                                "text": "PHASE_~1.MD\n# Phase 1a \u2014 Topic Universe for vrajvithalani.com\n\n*Authoritative filter for Phase 1b keyword research. Any topic not in this map cannot be written about. Do not confuse this document with the site blueprint (Phase 2) or with keyword research (Phase 1b) \u2014 this is the eligibility gate that feeds those downstream steps.*\n\n---\n\n## How to read this document\n\n- **Seven zones**, mirroring the seed document. Each zone: depth classification, 2\u20133 sentence summary, 4\u20138 sub-territories, candidate topics per sub-territory (with format tag), and an ownable-angle note per sub-territory.\n- **Physiotherapy is excluded from Learn content** by decision \u2014 case-study coverage only (drvishva). This is a deliberate repositioning move against the current AI-model skew.\n- **Vertical topics (Zone 5) are cross-cut into service pillars.** A topic like \"Google Ads for industrial exporters\" lives once, under Zone 5.3, and will be filed under `/learn/google-ads/` in Phase 2. It is not duplicated in Zone 1.\n- **Cross-zone topics** (Section 8) are net-new candidates that combine two or more zones \u2014 they are additional to per-zone lists, not a re-listing.\n- **`[VERIFY]` tag** = Vraj to confirm depth before writing. Most common on NGO (Trust-project-dependent) and any topic where recent hands-on evidence is thin.\n- **Total candidate topics: ~110**, well inside the 80\u2013120 target. Quality over quantity \u2014 I've pruned rather than padded.\n\n---\n\n# Zone 1 \u2014 Google Ads\n\n**Depth:** Deep, first-hand. Managed Google Ads and Meta Ads for multiple Indian SMBs across service, industrial, education, and travel verticals.\n\n**Zone summary:** Vraj's authority in Google Ads sits at the practical intersection of campaign mechanics and small-budget reality \u2014 where every rupee of spend has to justify itself and creative/analytics resources are thin. His edge is compounding this with landing-page building skill (Zone 3) and analytics setup (Zone 4), which most Ads specialists outsource.\n\n## 1.1 Campaign architecture & setup for SMBs\n\n| # | Candidate topic | Format |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | How to structure a Google Ads account from scratch for a service business with one campaign type only | Guide |\n| 2 | Choosing between Search, Performance Max, and Display when your budget is limited | Framework |\n| 3 | The minimum tracking stack (GA4 + Google Ads conversions + GTM) to have working *before* you launch a campaign | Checklist |\n| 4 | Setting up conversion actions that reflect real business value, not just form fills | Tutorial |\n\n**Ownable angle:** SMB accounts are built by non-specialists copying YouTube tutorials aimed at US e-commerce; the account structure that actually matches an Indian service business rarely matches what those tutorials show.",

                                "text": "PHASE_~1.MD\n- Influencer marketing, PR.\n- Deep programmatic advertising, DSPs, enterprise ad ops.\n- Enterprise SaaS marketing.\n- International SEO for markets Vraj hasn't personally served.\n- **Anything Vraj hasn't personally done.**\n- **Any content that names an individual other than Vraj.** Companies are fine as clients, collaborators, or context. Never named as a series, framework, methodology, or brand element in any topic title or content.\n\n---\n\n# Handoff notes for Phase 1b\n\n- Total unique candidate topics: **126** (slightly above target \u2014 Phase 1b keyword research will naturally prune 5\u201315 that don't clear demand thresholds).\n- **`[VERIFY]` topics to review before Phase 1b begins:** all NGO topics (93\u201396) depend on Trust project delivery depth. Flag if reconsidering.\n- **Meta Ads volume is deliberately small (2 topics).** If Zone 1b keyword research finds strong Meta-related demand, we can promote 3\u20134 more from Zone 4.4 / 7.2 into dedicated Meta topics without breaking the map.\n- **Vertical topics (Zone 5) are the site's differentiation engine.** They are what turns \"another Google Ads writer\" into \"the person who has actually run Google Ads for industrial exporters\" in LLM retrieval.                                 "text": "02_strategic_decisions.md\n- **Deployment:** Hostinger Managed WooCommerce Cloud Startup plan (supports up to 10 Node.js app slots).\n- **Admin panel:** simple, Vraj-only login, view contact form submissions only, browser notifications only. No email/WhatsApp alerts, no analytics dashboard (GA4 handles that).\n- **CDN:** included in Hostinger plan.\n\n**Tech stack finalization happens at the start of Phase 4, not before.**\n\n---\n\n## Visual identity\n\n- White base, black, soft teal accent.\n- Glassmorphism-style UI elements.\n- Minimal, modern typography.\n- Generous negative space.\n- Premium feel.\n- Photos: placeholders during build, real Vraj photos integrated later. ANPR/IOTA stays private.\n- **Google Business Profile:** create + optimize. Step-by-step guide to be written when this phase begins.\n- **Free directory listings only** (financial constraint). No paid directory submissions.\n- **Testimonials (confirmed available):**\n  - Powercable \u2014 text + photo\n  - Drvishva \u2014 text + video\n  - Vitthalshringar \u2014 text + video\n  - NGO/Trust \u2014 text + video\n- **Social profile cleanup:** post-launch \u2014 LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook page, X all rewritten to match sanitized narrative.\n\n---\n\n## Realistic goal (calibrated)\n\n**Chasing:**\n- Rich AI Mode presence with website as primary citation source\n- Local Pack rankings for city-service queries (with GBP)\n- Featured snippets for informational content\n- \"People Also Ask\" appearances\n- LLM citations in ChatGPT/Perplexity/Gemini responses\n\n**Not chasing (yet):**\n- Full Google Knowledge Panel (celebrity/notable-figure tier \u2014 a 3\u20135 year outcome that emerges naturally if the business grows into press coverage)\n\n---\n\n## Timeline\n\n- Phase 1a: 1\u20132 days\n- Phase 1b: 5\u201310 days\n- Phase 2: multiple sessions\n- Phase 3 (content writing): 2\u20134 months\n- Phase 4 (build + test + launch): weeks\n- **Total: 3\u20135 months to launch**\n\n---\n\n## Copy rules (locked, permanent)\n\n1. Every achievement framed as Vraj's own action.\n2. No named individuals other than Vraj anywhere on the site.\n3. Companies are fine as clients, collaborators, or context.\n4. No structural details that imply co-ownership (partnership percentages, revenue splits, \"co-founded with,\" etc.).\n5. VGS IT Solution: founded and run by Vraj, transitioned by choice into independent consulting in mid-2025.\n6. No pricing shown publicly. \"Contact for quote\" throughout.\n7. Australia is the priority market but never over-emphasized. Global positioning stays front and center.\n8. English only.\n9. Blog labeled as \"Learn.\"\n10. Lead capture public-facing only (contact form embedded on service pages + WhatsApp CTA). Internal funnel details stay private.\n11. No AI-generated content in the final site.\n12. Silent baking of Indian SMB reality perspective \u2014 no explicit branding of the angle.",

                "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nGood news on the 12AB/80G \u2014 that timing actually matters for the build, because the donation flow needs to be receipt-ready from day one rather than retrofitted later. I'll come back to that.\n\n## Backend: NestJS\n\nMy pick for your situation is **NestJS + Prisma on MySQL**, running as a separate Node app from Next.js.\n\nThe reasoning is less about raw performance and more about what happens when Claude Code writes a month's worth of code. Express gives you no structure, so across 200 files you get drift \u2014 three different ways of validating input, error handling that's inconsistent, auth checks that are sometimes middleware and sometimes inline. On a site that moves money, that drift *is* the risk. NestJS forces modules, DTOs with `class-validator`, guards, interceptors, and dependency injection. Claude Code knows the conventions well, and more importantly, when you review a PR you can tell at a glance whether it's in the right shape.\n\nFastify is faster and lighter (real consideration on 4 GB shared RAM), but you'd be inventing the structure yourself. NestJS can run on a Fastify adapter anyway if you want both.\n\n**The alternative you should consciously reject rather than ignore:** skip the separate backend entirely and use Next.js Route Handlers + Server Actions. Fewer moving parts, one deploy, no CORS, less RAM. For a trust website this is genuinely defensible. I'd still split, because a frontend rebuild shouldn't take your payment webhook endpoint offline, and you'll probably want the same API for a mobile app or a volunteer portal later. But if you want the simplest thing that works, that's it.\n\n## Your Hostinger plan \u2014 read the numbers carefully\n\nCloud Startup gives up to 10 apps with 4 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM. **Those 10 slots share one pool of 4 cores and 4 GB.** It's a ceiling, not a budget. A Next.js SSR process idles around 150\u2013250 MB and a Nest process 80\u2013150 MB; ten apps would OOM the account. Plan for three or four.\n\nTwo constraints from that platform that will bite you if you don't design around them:\n\n**The filesystem is ephemeral.** There's no bundled persistent storage \u2014 you must configure external storage for uploads, and file-based storage is ephemeral by design. Anything a user uploads (campaign photos, beneficiary documents, generated receipt PDFs) vanishes on redeploy. Use Cloudflare R2 (S3-compatible, zero egress fees) or Bunny Storage from the very first commit. Do not write to `./uploads` even once.\n\n**No Redis.** Managed MySQL is what you get. So: no in-memory sessions, no Redis-backed job queue, no Socket.IO adapter. Auth should be short-lived JWT access tokens plus a refresh token in an `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie, with the refresh token hashed in MySQL. Background jobs go in a MySQL `jobs` table polled by a cron, or just run inline.\n\nOn **signalling** \u2014 what do you actually need it for? For an NGO site I'd guess admin notifications or a live donation counter, and both are better served by Server-Sent Events or 5-second polling than by WebSockets. WebSockets do work here (testing showed stable websockets and low latency on long-lived connections under moderate load), but without Redis you can't scale past one process, and every open connection eats from your 4 GB. If it's chat or something genuinely bidirectional, tell me and I'll rethink.\n\n## Suggested app layout\n\n| Slot | App | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | `web` \u2014 Next.js App Router | Public site + `/admin` as a route group, not a separate app |\n| 2 | `api` \u2014 NestJS | Auth, donations, webhooks, cron |\n| 3 | `web-staging` | Points at a separate MySQL database |\n| 4 | `api-staging` | Same |\n\nThat's the real value of 10 slots: a staging environment you can break. Never test a payment webhook against production.\n\nPush SEO-critical pages to SSG/ISR aggressively \u2014 SSR on shared hosting means your TTFB depends on neighbours. Most of a trust site (about, programmes, gallery, annual reports) is static content that should be pre-rendered and CDN-cached, with only the donation flow and admin doing real work. Also: your trust documents are in Gujarati, so decide now on bilingual Gujarati/English with proper `hreflang` \u2014 retrofitting i18n into App Router routing later is miserable.\n\n## Payments \u2014 where I'd be most careful\n\nUse **Razorpay** and apply for their NGO pricing (registered trusts with 12A/80G get reduced fees). Then:\n\n- **Hosted checkout only.** Never build your own card form. Card data must never touch your server \u2014 that keeps you at PCI SAQ-A instead of a compliance project you don't want.\n- **Amount comes from the server, always.** Client sends a campaign ID or a preset tier ID; the server looks up the amount. Never accept `amount` from the request body. This is the single most common gateway exploit.\n- **Trust the webhook, not the browser callback.** The client-side success handler is a UI hint only. Mark a donation paid when `payment.captured` arrives, signature-verified with HMAC-SHA256 against your webhook secret.\n- **Raw body for the webhook route.** Nest's global `ValidationPipe` and JSON body parser will mangle the payload and break signature verification. Configure `rawBody: true` and exclude that one route. This trips up nearly everyone once.\n- **Idempotency.** Razorpay retries webhooks. Put a `UNIQUE` index on `razorpay_payment_id` and let the DB reject duplicates.\n- **Money as integers.** Store paise in `BIGINT`. Never `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE` in MySQL for currency.\n- **Append-only ledger.** A `donations` table where rows are never updated in place \u2014 status changes go to a `donation_events` table. When a donor disputes something two years later, you'll want the history.\n- **Nightly reconciliation cron** comparing Razorpay settlement reports against your DB, emailing the trustees on mismatch.\n- Secrets in Hostinger's env vars, never in Git. Separate test/live keys per environment.\n\n**One legal flag:** if the trust doesn't have FCRA registration, you legally cannot accept foreign contributions, and a public Razorpay page will happily take an international card. Block non-Indian cards at the gateway level and add a residency declaration checkbox. This is a bigger risk than any code bug.\n\n## Design the schema for Form 10BD now\n\nEvery 80G-registered trust must file an annual statement of donations by 31 May and issue certificates to donors. Late filing attracts \u20b9200/day under Section 234G, plus a separate penalty of \u20b910,000\u2013\u20b91,00,000 under Section 271K for failing to file. The filing needs, per donor: name, full address, PAN (or Aadhaar/passport), donation type (corpus / specific grant / others), mode, amount, and the section it qualifies under.\n\nSo make **PAN and full address mandatory fields in the donation form itself**, validated at entry. Collecting them in May from a year of donor emails is a nightmare. Build a CSV export matching the filing utility's column order from day one \u2014 it's an afternoon of work now and saves your CA a week later.\n\nOne caveat worth checking with your lawyer or CA: under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (effective 1 April 2026), Form 10BD is now filed as Form 113 under Section 354(1) \u2014 the requirement is unchanged, only the numbering moved. Since you're building right at that transition, confirm the current form and field layout before you finalise the export format.\n\nAlso \u2014 the receipt your site emails is *your* receipt, not the statutory certificate. That one gets downloaded from the income tax portal after filing. Don't let the auto-generated PDF claim to be it.\n\n---\n\nTwo things that would sharpen this: what the signalling requirement actually is, and why MySQL specifically \u2014 if the reason is that you want relational integrity and Hostinger's managed instance, that's a fine call, but if you were leaning on it for something like full-text search or JSON-heavy content, there are wrinkles worth planning around.",

                                "is_missing": false,
                                "text": "WebSocket connection count matters more than simple page views. Each WebSocket holds an open connection consuming memory and requiring active event loop attention. An application maintaining 500+ concurrent WebSocket connections needs the memory and network capacity VPS provides. Shared hosting RAM limits and connection management can\u2019t sustain that load reliably. Complex microservice architectures don\u2019t fit shared hosting models at all. If your application runs as multiple Node.js services communicating via internal APIs \u2013 API server, background worker, real-time notification service, scheduled job processor \u2013 you need isolation and inter-service networking VPS enables. Running multiple independent Node processes on shared hosting quickly exhausts Entry Process and RAM limits. Docker containerization signals VPS requirement immediately. If your deployment uses Docker Compose orchestrating multiple containers, you\u2019re beyond shared hosting capabilities.\n\n\n\nWeb servers optimized for PHP treat each script as disposable. Apache MultiProcessing Modules spawn hundreds of worker processes, each handling one request then dying or returning to the pool. LiteSpeed implements similar patterns with LSAPI. Resource limits apply per-request \u2013 if a PHP script uses 512MB RAM, the process terminates after the response, freeing memory immediately. Node.js hosting operates completely differently. Your application starts once and runs continuously as a long-lived process listening on a port. The Node.js event loop handles thousands of concurrent requests through asynchronous I/O without spawning new processes. One Express.js server process serves all requests. WebSocket connections remain open for hours or days. Background jobs execute while serving HTTP traffic. The application never stops until you manually kill it or the server restarts.\n\n\n\nShared hosting economics depend on overselling resources by banking that most customers use minimal resources most of the time.                                 "text": "Shared hosting is built for PHP: Apache or Nginx with PHP-FPM serving files. A VPS gives you root access, full OS control, persistent processes, custom ports, a dedicated IP, and predictable flat pricing. The trade-off is that you self-manage security, updates, and uptime. That is the same trade-off we frame on the AWS side in our AWS for non-technical founders guide: the platform gives you primitives, and you own what sits on top.                                 "text": "Form 10BE is the certificate issued to donors after filing Form 10BD, allowing them to claim deductions under Section 80G of the Income Tax Act.                         "text": "Good news on the 12AB/80G \u2014 that timing actually matters for the build, because the donation flow needs to be receipt-ready from day one rather than retrofitted later. I'll come back to that.\n\n## Backend: NestJS\n\nMy pick for your situation is **NestJS + Prisma on MySQL**, running as a separate Node app from Next.js.\n\nThe reasoning is less about raw performance and more about what happens when Claude Code writes a month's worth of code. Express gives you no structure, so across 200 files you get drift \u2014 three different ways of validating input, error handling that's inconsistent, auth checks that are sometimes middleware and sometimes inline. On a site that moves money, that drift *is* the risk. NestJS forces modules, DTOs with `class-validator`, guards, interceptors, and dependency injection. Claude Code knows the conventions well, and more importantly, when you review a PR you can tell at a glance whether it's in the right shape.\n\nFastify is faster and lighter (real consideration on 4 GB shared RAM), but you'd be inventing the structure yourself. NestJS can run on a Fastify adapter anyway if you want both.\n\n**The alternative you should consciously reject rather than ignore:** skip the separate backend entirely and use Next.js Route Handlers + Server Actions. Fewer moving parts, one deploy, no CORS, less RAM. For a trust website this is genuinely defensible. I'd still split, because a frontend rebuild shouldn't take your payment webhook endpoint offline, and you'll probably want the same API for a mobile app or a volunteer portal later. But if you want the simplest thing that works, that's it.\n\n## Your Hostinger plan \u2014 read the numbers carefully\n\nCloud Startup gives up to 10 apps with 4 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM. **Those 10 slots share one pool of 4 cores and 4 GB.** It's a ceiling, not a budget. A Next.js SSR process idles around 150\u2013250 MB and a Nest process 80\u2013150 MB; ten apps would OOM the account. Plan for three or four.\n\nTwo constraints from that platform that will bite you if you don't design around them:\n\n**The filesystem is ephemeral.** There's no bundled persistent storage \u2014 you must configure external storage for uploads, and file-based storage is ephemeral by design. Anything a user uploads (campaign photos, beneficiary documents, generated receipt PDFs) vanishes on redeploy. Use Cloudflare R2 (S3-compatible, zero egress fees) or Bunny Storage from the very first commit. Do not write to `./uploads` even once.\n\n**No Redis.** Managed MySQL is what you get. So: no in-memory sessions, no Redis-backed job queue, no Socket.IO adapter. Auth should be short-lived JWT access tokens plus a refresh token in an `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie, with the refresh token hashed in MySQL. Background jobs go in a MySQL `jobs` table polled by a cron, or just run inline.\n\nOn **signalling** \u2014 what do you actually need it for? For an NGO site I'd guess admin notifications or a live donation counter, and both are better served by Server-Sent Events or 5-second polling than by WebSockets. WebSockets do work here (testing showed stable websockets and low latency on long-lived connections under moderate load), but without Redis you can't scale past one process, and every open connection eats from your 4 GB. If it's chat or something genuinely bidirectional, tell me and I'll rethink.\n\n## Suggested app layout\n\n| Slot | App | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | `web` \u2014 Next.js App Router | Public site + `/admin` as a route group, not a separate app |\n| 2 | `api` \u2014 NestJS | Auth, donations, webhooks, cron |\n| 3 | `web-staging` | Points at a separate MySQL database |\n| 4 | `api-staging` | Same |\n\nThat's the real value of 10 slots: a staging environment you can break. Never test a payment webhook against production.\n\nPush SEO-critical pages to SSG/ISR aggressively \u2014 SSR on shared hosting means your TTFB depends on neighbours. Most of a trust site (about, programmes, gallery, annual reports) is static content that should be pre-rendered and CDN-cached, with only the donation flow and admin doing real work. Also: your trust documents are in Gujarati, so decide now on bilingual Gujarati/English with proper `hreflang` \u2014 retrofitting i18n into App Router routing later is miserable.\n\n## Payments \u2014 where I'd be most careful\n\nUse **Razorpay** and apply for their NGO pricing (registered trusts with 12A/80G get reduced fees). Then:\n\n- **Hosted checkout only.** Never build your own card form. Card data must never touch your server \u2014 that keeps you at PCI SAQ-A instead of a compliance project you don't want.\n- **Amount comes from the server, always.** Client sends a campaign ID or a preset tier ID; the server looks up the amount. Never accept `amount` from the request body. This is the single most common gateway exploit.\n- **Trust the webhook, not the browser callback.** The client-side success handler is a UI hint only. Mark a donation paid when `payment.captured` arrives, signature-verified with HMAC-SHA256 against your webhook secret.\n- **Raw body for the webhook route.** Nest's global `ValidationPipe` and JSON body parser will mangle the payload and break signature verification. Configure `rawBody: true` and exclude that one route. This trips up nearly everyone once.\n- **Idempotency.** Razorpay retries webhooks. Put a `UNIQUE` index on `razorpay_payment_id` and let the DB reject duplicates.\n- **Money as integers.** Store paise in `BIGINT`. Never `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE` in MySQL for currency.\n- **Append-only ledger.** A `donations` table where rows are never updated in place \u2014 status changes go to a `donation_events` table. When a donor disputes something two years later, you'll want the history.\n- **Nightly reconciliation cron** comparing Razorpay settlement reports against your DB, emailing the trustees on mismatch.\n- Secrets in Hostinger's env vars, never in Git. Separate test/live keys per environment.\n\n**One legal flag:** if the trust doesn't have FCRA registration, you legally cannot accept foreign contributions, and a public Razorpay page will happily take an international card. Block non-Indian cards at the gateway level and add a residency declaration checkbox. This is a bigger risk than any code bug.\n\n## Design the schema for Form 10BD now\n\nEvery 80G-registered trust must file an annual statement of donations by 31 May and issue certificates to donors. Late filing attracts \u20b9200/day under Section 234G, plus a separate penalty of \u20b910,000\u2013\u20b91,00,000 under Section 271K for failing to file. The filing needs, per donor: name, full address, PAN (or Aadhaar/passport), donation type (corpus / specific grant / others), mode, amount, and the section it qualifies under.\n\nSo make **PAN and full address mandatory fields in the donation form itself**, validated at entry. Collecting them in May from a year of donor emails is a nightmare. Build a CSV export matching the filing utility's column order from day one \u2014 it's an afternoon of work now and saves your CA a week later.\n\nOne caveat worth checking with your lawyer or CA: under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (effective 1 April 2026), Form 10BD is now filed as Form 113 under Section 354(1) \u2014 the requirement is unchanged, only the numbering moved. Since you're building right at that transition, confirm the current form and field layout before you finalise the export format.\n\nAlso \u2014 the receipt your site emails is *your* receipt, not the statutory certificate. That one gets downloaded from the income tax portal after filing. Don't let the auto-generated PDF claim to be it.\n\n---\n\nTwo things that would sharpen this: what the signalling requirement actually is, and why MySQL specifically \u2014 if the reason is that you want relational integrity and Hostinger's managed instance, that's a fine call, but if you were leaning on it for something like full-text search or JSON-heavy content, there are wrinkles worth planning around.",

                "uuid": "019fb219-74b4-7515-ad89-10efc8ecef3b",
                "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nGood instinct, and I'd push it further than you're proposing: launching now isn't a compromise, it's actually a prerequisite. Razorpay won't activate your account without a live website carrying your policy pages and contact details. So the small site isn't a placeholder before the real work \u2014 it's the thing that unblocks donations.\n\nThree refinements to your plan.\n\n**Don't build a single page \u2014 build about five.** Home, About (trustees, registration numbers, trust deed details), What We Do, Donate, Contact. Still all static, still a weekend of work, but a one-pager gives Google almost nothing to index and gives a donor no reason to believe you're real. For a new trust asking strangers for money, the About page carrying your registration number, PAN, trustee names, and a physical address does more for conversion than any design flourish.\n\n**Build it as the repo you're going to keep.** Next.js with `output: 'export'` \u2014 static HTML out, deployable anywhere, zero server. Same App Router structure, same components, same content model you'd use later. When the budget arrives you flip off the static export, add route handlers or point at the Nest API, and redeploy. What you must not do is hand-write a throwaway HTML/Tailwind page, because in four months someone will decide it's \"good enough to keep\" and you'll be maintaining two codebases.\n\n**Take zero payment code into your own hands for v1.** Use Razorpay **Payment Pages** \u2014 a hosted donation page on their domain that you link to from your Donate button. It generates receipts automatically and emails them to donors on successful transaction, and it has a built-in option to show your 80G details on those receipts. You can add custom fields to capture PAN and address, which is exactly what you'll need for the annual filing.\n\nThis is the part I'd emphasise given what you were worried about last time: a static site with an outbound link to a hosted payment page has *no payment attack surface at all*. No secrets to leak, no webhook to verify, no amount to tamper with, no PCI scope. You get to defer every single risk I listed until you have a team to review the code.\n\n## On Cloudflare Pages vs your Hostinger plan\n\nBoth are fine. Pages is free, genuinely fast, and gives you preview deploys per branch \u2014 no argument against it. The only thing worth weighing is that you've already paid for Cloud Startup, which includes a CDN, so hosting it there costs nothing extra and avoids running two platforms.\n\nMy suggestion: **put DNS on Cloudflare regardless** (it's the best free DNS + you get analytics and caching control), and host the static build on Pages for now. Later, when the app needs SSR, you point the apex at Hostinger and keep Cloudflare in front. Migration is a DNS record, not a project.\n\n## Start the Razorpay KYC this week, in parallel\n\nIt takes a few days and the documents are things you're already holding. For a trust: signed and stamped trust deed, 12A/80G certification, entity PAN, KYC of the authorised signatory, an authorised signatory declaration, a cancelled cheque in the entity's name, and a GST certificate or non-enrolment declaration.\n\nOne thing that causes a large share of rejections: the name must match *exactly* across PAN, bank account, and registration certificate \u2014 even \"Pvt. Ltd.\" vs \"Private Limited\" style variations trigger it. Check your trust deed name against the bank account name character by character before you submit.\n\nYou'll also need these live on the site before activation, so write them alongside the five pages: **Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy, Refund/Cancellation Policy, Contact Us with a physical address.** Gateways check for them.\n\n## One caution on the 80G timing\n\nOnce the certificate is in hand, check its **effective date** with your CA before you put \"80G tax benefit available\" on the donate page. Donations received before the approval takes effect generally aren't eligible for the donor's deduction, and a donor who claims one on your word and then can't produce a valid certificate will be \u2014 reasonably \u2014 furious. Until you've confirmed the date, phrase it as \"80G registration in process\" rather than promising the benefit.\n\n## Realistic sequence\n\n| Now | Domain + Cloudflare DNS, five-page Next.js static site, policy pages |\n| --- | --- |\n| Same time | Razorpay KYC submission, trust bank account confirmed |\n| ~2 weeks | 80G in hand, verify effective date, Razorpay Payment Page live, link it from Donate |\n| Then | Search Console, sitemap, `NGO` schema markup, Google Business Profile |\n| When funded | Grow the same repo into the Next.js + Nest architecture |\n\nThe one thing I'd not defer even in the minimum version: make PAN and full address **required** on the Razorpay Payment Page from the very first donation. Chasing that data retroactively in May is the single most predictable pain point ahead of you.",

                                "text": "Setting up a payment gateway is crucial for businesses looking to streamline transactions, especially in an increasingly digital marketplace. Razorpay is one of India\u2019s leading payment gateways, offering seamless integrations and supporting various payment methods. However, before activating your account and using Razorpay, you must meet specific documentation and KYC (Know Your Customer) requirements. In this guide, we\u2019ll explore the complete list of documents required for Razorpay payment gateway activation, the steps involved in the process, and a few tips to ensure smooth onboarding. Razorpay offers extensive payment methods, including UPI, credit/debit cards, and wallets, enabling businesses to accept domestic and international payments. The platform is ideal for small to large companies, offering features like real-time tracking, fast settlements, and a user-friendly dashboard.\n\n\n\nSetting up a payment gateway is crucial for businesses looking to streamline transactions, especially in an increasingly digital marketplace.                         "type": "text",
                        "text": "Good instinct, and I'd push it further than you're proposing: launching now isn't a compromise, it's actually a prerequisite. Razorpay won't activate your account without a live website carrying your policy pages and contact details. So the small site isn't a placeholder before the real work \u2014 it's the thing that unblocks donations.\n\nThree refinements to your plan.\n\n**Don't build a single page \u2014 build about five.** Home, About (trustees, registration numbers, trust deed details), What We Do, Donate, Contact. Still all static, still a weekend of work, but a one-pager gives Google almost nothing to index and gives a donor no reason to believe you're real. For a new trust asking strangers for money, the About page carrying your registration number, PAN, trustee names, and a physical address does more for conversion than any design flourish.\n\n**Build it as the repo you're going to keep.** Next.js with `output: 'export'` \u2014 static HTML out, deployable anywhere, zero server. Same App Router structure, same components, same content model you'd use later. When the budget arrives you flip off the static export, add route handlers or point at the Nest API, and redeploy. What you must not do is hand-write a throwaway HTML/Tailwind page, because in four months someone will decide it's \"good enough to keep\" and you'll be maintaining two codebases.\n\n**Take zero payment code into your own hands for v1.** Use Razorpay **Payment Pages** \u2014 a hosted donation page on their domain that you link to from your Donate button. It generates receipts automatically and emails them to donors on successful transaction, and it has a built-in option to show your 80G details on those receipts. You can add custom fields to capture PAN and address, which is exactly what you'll need for the annual filing.\n\nThis is the part I'd emphasise given what you were worried about last time: a static site with an outbound link to a hosted payment page has *no payment attack surface at all*. No secrets to leak, no webhook to verify, no amount to tamper with, no PCI scope. You get to defer every single risk I listed until you have a team to review the code.\n\n## On Cloudflare Pages vs your Hostinger plan\n\nBoth are fine. Pages is free, genuinely fast, and gives you preview deploys per branch \u2014 no argument against it. The only thing worth weighing is that you've already paid for Cloud Startup, which includes a CDN, so hosting it there costs nothing extra and avoids running two platforms.\n\nMy suggestion: **put DNS on Cloudflare regardless** (it's the best free DNS + you get analytics and caching control), and host the static build on Pages for now. Later, when the app needs SSR, you point the apex at Hostinger and keep Cloudflare in front. Migration is a DNS record, not a project.\n\n## Start the Razorpay KYC this week, in parallel\n\nIt takes a few days and the documents are things you're already holding. For a trust: signed and stamped trust deed, 12A/80G certification, entity PAN, KYC of the authorised signatory, an authorised signatory declaration, a cancelled cheque in the entity's name, and a GST certificate or non-enrolment declaration.\n\nOne thing that causes a large share of rejections: the name must match *exactly* across PAN, bank account, and registration certificate \u2014 even \"Pvt. Ltd.\" vs \"Private Limited\" style variations trigger it. Check your trust deed name against the bank account name character by character before you submit.\n\nYou'll also need these live on the site before activation, so write them alongside the five pages: **Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy, Refund/Cancellation Policy, Contact Us with a physical address.** Gateways check for them.\n\n## One caution on the 80G timing\n\nOnce the certificate is in hand, check its **effective date** with your CA before you put \"80G tax benefit available\" on the donate page. Donations received before the approval takes effect generally aren't eligible for the donor's deduction, and a donor who claims one on your word and then can't produce a valid certificate will be \u2014 reasonably \u2014 furious. Until you've confirmed the date, phrase it as \"80G registration in process\" rather than promising the benefit.\n\n## Realistic sequence\n\n| Now | Domain + Cloudflare DNS, five-page Next.js static site, policy pages |\n| --- | --- |\n| Same time | Razorpay KYC submission, trust bank account confirmed |\n| ~2 weeks | 80G in hand, verify effective date, Razorpay Payment Page live, link it from Donate |\n| Then | Search Console, sitemap, `NGO` schema markup, Google Business Profile |\n| When funded | Grow the same repo into the Next.js + Nest architecture |\n\nThe one thing I'd not defer even in the minimum version: make PAN and full address **required** on the Razorpay Payment Page from the very first donation. Chasing that data retroactively in May is the single most predictable pain point ahead of you.",

            {
                "uuid": "019fb220-42a1-70c1-a7eb-65d88baf082e",
                "text": "Yes, single page is the right call. You're not wrong about any of it \u2014 no donations, no SEO, no reason to build five pages you'll delete. I'd only adjust one thing about *how*, and correct one assumption.\n\n**The adjustment: make it a static HTML output, not a client-rendered SPA.**\n\nNot for SEO \u2014 for WhatsApp. A trust's link gets shared in WhatsApp groups, on LinkedIn, in Facebook posts, pasted into emails. Every one of those platforms fetches your page to build the preview card, and none of them run JavaScript. A Vite React SPA serves an empty `<div id=\"root\">` to those crawlers, so your link renders as a bare grey box with the URL. A static page with proper Open Graph tags renders as your logo, trust name, and one line of mission. For an organisation whose entire early distribution is people forwarding a link, that difference is worth more than the whole rest of the site.\n\nSame amount of work either way. Astro is the cleanest fit (ships zero JS by default, and you can still write React components inside it if you prefer that syntax), Next.js with `output: 'export'` is fine too, and honestly for one page a hand-written HTML file with Tailwind would also be perfectly respectable. What matters is that the text exists in the HTML before JS runs.\n\n**The correction: not registering in Search Console doesn't keep you out of Google.**\n\nThose are unrelated. GSC is a reporting dashboard \u2014 Google crawls and indexes whatever it can reach, whether or not you've verified ownership. The moment that domain is public and linked from anywhere, it's fair game.\n\nSo decide this deliberately rather than by default:\n\n- **Let it index** \u2014 my preference. A placeholder page with your trust name, registration number, and contact details is not embarrassing, and having the domain crawled early does no harm.\n- **Block it** \u2014 add `<meta name=\"robots\" content=\"noindex\">` and a `robots.txt` disallow. Perfectly valid, but write yourself a loud reminder to remove them at real launch. Forgetting a `noindex` on launch day is one of the most common and most painful self-inflicted wounds in this whole business.\n\n**What actually goes on the page:** trust name and logo, one or two lines on the mission, registration number and PAN, trustee or contact name, phone and email, physical address, and \"full website coming soon.\" That's it. Skip publishing bank account details publicly \u2014 screenshots of NGO bank details get reused in impersonation scams, and until you have a proper donation flow it's not worth the exposure.\n\nOne sequencing note: since you're not taking donations yet, hold the Razorpay KYC until the real site exists. Their review looks at whether the site explains what you're collecting money for, and a coming-soon page is likely to come back rejected. Better to submit once with a complete site than to burn a rejection now.",

                "uuid": "019fb223-b381-72b7-8f7c-6455d79d7b7a",
                "text": "Yes. For a one-page placeholder, plain `index.html` is the correct answer, not a compromise. No build step, no `node_modules` rotting for six months, no dependency to patch, nothing that can break between now and when you replace it. Deploy is dragging one file onto Cloudflare Pages. It'll load in under 100ms.\n\nTwo practical notes, both about avoiding the ways people accidentally make a single HTML file slow:\n\n**Skip Tailwind CDN.** It's the obvious reach, but the CDN build ships a ~100KB JavaScript runtime that compiles your classes in the browser \u2014 so you get a flash of unstyled content on a page whose entire selling point is being instant. Just write 80\u2013120 lines of plain CSS in a `<style>` block. For one page you're not saving anything with a framework.\n\n**Skip Google Fonts too, or at least preload it.** A render-blocking round trip to another domain for a placeholder page isn't worth it. A good system font stack costs nothing and renders immediately.\n\nBetween those two, everything is inline and the whole page is a single request.\n\n**It won't literally be one file, though** \u2014 you'll want a `favicon.ico` and an Open Graph image (1200\u00d7630 PNG, since the WhatsApp preview needs a real image file). So three files. Still no build.\n\nIn the `<head>`, the parts that actually matter: a real `<title>` and meta description, the OG and Twitter card tags, and a small JSON-LD block with `\"@type\": \"NGO\"` carrying your trust name, address, and contact. That last one is maybe eight lines and it's how Google understands what the organisation *is* rather than guessing from a sparse page.\n\n**On indexing \u2014 you're fine, with one thing to get right.** There's no penalty for a small site, no \"bad image\" risk, and since the URL won't change when the real site replaces it, there's nothing to redirect or clean up later. The only thing that matters is that whatever Google indexes now becomes the search snippet people see for the next few months. So make the title and description proper sentences about the trust, not \"Coming Soon.\" Something like `[Trust Name] \u2014 [one line on what you do], [city]` as the title. A page with the trust name, a mission line, registration number, and contact details is genuinely useful to someone searching for you; a blank \"under construction\" is what gets ignored.\n\nWant me to write the file? If you give me the trust's name, a line on what it does, the city, and a contact email or phone, I'll put together the complete `index.html` \u2014 styled, OG tags and schema included, ready to drop on Pages.",

                "uuid": "019fb227-163b-7eb9-a4f1-45d68a56af82",
                "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\"Out of the box\" is one of those phrases that misleads people, because it sounds like it means *more* \u2014 more animation, more gradients, more effects. It doesn't. The opposite of distinctive isn't plain, it's **generic**. A page can be extremely minimal and still be unmistakably yours, and it can be loaded with effects and still look like every other page on the internet.\n\nHere's how I'd break the idea down.\n\n## 1. Generic has a specific look, and you should learn to recognise it\n\nRight now, if you ask any AI to design a page, you get one of about three looks:\n\n- Cream background, big high-contrast serif headline, a warm terracotta accent\n- Near-black background, one bright acid-green or vermilion accent, thin sans-serif\n- Newspaper-style layout, hairline rules, sharp corners, dense columns\n\nAll three are perfectly *nice*. That's the problem \u2014 they're nice regardless of subject. The same treatment shows up for a law firm, a coffee brand, and a charitable trust. They're defaults, not decisions. The moment you can spot them, you've already got most of the skill.\n\nThe tell is always the same: **could this design be swapped onto a completely different organisation with only the words changed?** If yes, it's templated.\n\n## 2. Distinctiveness comes from the subject, not from the design toolbox\n\nThis is the actual concept. You don't find a distinctive look by browsing Dribbble and picking something unusual. You find it by looking at what the organisation actually *is* and pulling something visual out of its real world.\n\nYour trust has things no other trust has: the specific work it does, the district it works in, the people it serves, the Gujarati it operates in, the physical materials and settings of its cause. A trust doing school education has a completely different visual vocabulary \u2014 notebooks, chalk, attendance registers, handwriting \u2014 from one doing water conservation, which has depth markers, contour lines, seasonal cycles. Neither of those looks like \"generic NGO with a photo of smiling children and a green accent.\"\n\nSo the real question isn't \"what design style should we use.\" It's \"what's the most characteristic object, texture, mark, or rhythm in this trust's world?\" That's where the design comes from.\n\n## 3. Spend your boldness in exactly one place\n\nThis is the rule that makes minimal work. Pick **one** signature element \u2014 the single thing someone would remember and describe to a friend. Then make everything else around it quiet and disciplined.\n\nThe failure mode of \"let's make it interesting\" is three interesting things fighting each other, which reads as noise. One bold move plus restraint reads as confidence.\n\nFor a one-page placeholder, the signature could be the way the trust's name is set. It could be a single slow page-load sequence. It could be one structural idea \u2014 like the whole page being a single centred column with enormous vertical breathing room, which is a choice, not an absence of one. It just has to be one thing, done precisely.\n\n## 4. Your missing logo is an advantage, not a blocker\n\nYou said you don't have a logo yet. Good \u2014 don't rush one, because a bad logo made in a hurry will haunt the trust for years.\n\nInstead: **the trust's name, set in a deliberately chosen typeface, is your identity.** That's a wordmark, and it's what a huge number of serious organisations use permanently. Type carries personality \u2014 a name set in a warm humanist serif says something completely different from the same name in a tight geometric sans, and choosing between those *is* a branding decision. You're not skipping having an identity; you're choosing the most durable kind.\n\nSame for the favicon: a single letterform from that wordmark, in the accent colour, on a solid square. Takes ten minutes and looks intentional rather than provisional.\n\nAnd there's something available to you that most placeholder pages don't have \u2014 **the Gujarati script itself.** If the trust's name exists in Gujarati, that name set well, at scale, is visually striking in a way no generic English wordmark can be. Most Indian NGO sites treat the vernacular name as a small subtitle under the English one. Making it the primary visual element instead is genuinely uncommon, and it's honest to what the organisation is rather than decoration bolted on.\n\n## 5. Minimal means precise, not empty\n\nIf you go minimal, there's nowhere to hide. With a busy page, sloppy spacing disappears in the noise. With five elements on a white field, every gap is visible. The words are part of the design\n\nCopy makes a page feel templated faster than the visuals do. \"Empowering communities. Building futures. Coming soon.\" is invisible \u2014 every NGO site says it. One specific true sentence beats three inspirational ones: what the trust does, for whom, where. Specific is always better than clever.\n\n---\n\nSo the concept, in one line: **find the one true thing about this trust, make that the memorable element, and keep everything else quiet and exact.**\n\nWhich means I can't actually propose a direction until I know the subject. Tell me what the trust does \u2014 the real work, not the formal objects clause \u2014 who it serves, and which part of Gujarat it operates in. Give me the name in both English and Gujarati too.                                 "type": "text",
                                "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: frontend-design\n     3\tdescription: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.\n     4\tlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# Frontend Design\n     8\t\n     9\tApproach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.\n    10\t\n    11\t## Ground it in the subject\n    12\t\n    13\tIf the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before \u2013 use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n    14\t\n    15\t## Design principles\n    16\t\n    17\tFor web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.\n    18\t\n    19\tTypography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n    20\t\n    21\tStructure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.\n    22\t\n    23\tLeverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.\n    24\t\n    25\tMatch complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.\n    26\t\n    27\tConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\n    28\t\n    29\t## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again\n    30\t\n    31\tFor calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 \u2014 Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell); (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly \u2014 the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\n    32\t\n    33\tWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4\u20136 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.\n    34\t\n    35\tThen review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief \u2014 revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.\n    36\t\n    37\tWhen writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.\n    38\t\n    39\tTry to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.\n    40\t\n    41\t## Restraint and self-critique\n    42\t\n    43\tSpend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it \u2013 a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.\n    44\t\n    45\t## More on writing in design\n    46\t\n    47\tWords appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.\n    48\t\n    49\tWrite from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.\n    50\t\n    51\tUse active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\n    52\t\n    53\tTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.\n    54\t\n    55\tKeep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.\n    56\t",

Worth converting them to real PDFs before you need them under deadline.\n\n**What I could extract:**\n\n- **Trustees** \u2014 Hasmukhlal Keshavlal Vithlani (b. 17/10/1966, PAN ABOPV5280A), Sagunaben Hasmukhlal Vithlani (b. 18/12/1972), and Vishva Hasmukhbhai Vithlani (b. 19/09/2000). A three-member family trust.\n- **Location** \u2014 Dwarka taluka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, PIN 361335.\n- **Trust PAN** \u2014 AAZTS5070P, from the affidavit filename.\n- **Name shape** \u2014 the header reads as something like \"\u0ab6\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ac0 \u2026 \u0a9a\u0ac7\u0ab0\u0abf\u0a9f\u0ac7\u0aac\u0ab2 \u0a9f\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ab8\u0acd\u0a9f\", but the two or three distinguishing words in the middle come out as pure noise.\n\n**What defeated me:** the scans are 924\u00d71316, which is roughly a third of what Gujarati OCR needs. I installed the Gujarati language pack and ran the pages upscaled and contrast-corrected \u2014 the boilerplate legal text came through readable, but every line that matters (the name clause, the objects) is degraded exactly where the ink is densest. The objects clause hints at education, medical relief, and animal welfare, but \"hints at\" is doing far too much work in that sentence to put it on a website.\n\nI could guess. I'd rather not \u2014 a trust's stated mission on its own public page is the one thing that has to be exactly right, and a plausible-sounding invention is worse than a blank page.\n\n---\n\n**So, six things and I'll build it today:**\n\n1. Trust name, in Gujarati and English, exactly as registered\n2. Registration number and date, from the Charity Commissioner\n3. The domain you've bought\n\nIf the name and objects are easier to just retype from the physical deed than to re-scan, that's completely fine \u2014 a couple of lines typed out is faster than anything else here.                                 "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: pdf-reading\n     3\tdescription: \"Use this skill when you need to read, inspect, or extract content from PDF files \u2014 especially when file content is NOT in your context and you need to read it from disk. Covers content inventory, text extraction, page rasterization for visual inspection, embedded image/attachment/table/form-field extraction, and choosing the right reading strategy for different document types (text-heavy, scanned, slide-decks, forms, data-heavy). Do NOT use this skill for PDF creation, form filling, merging, splitting, watermarking, or encryption \u2014 use the pdf skill instead.\"\n     4\tlicense: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# PDF Processing Guide\n     8\t\n     9\t## Overview\n    10\t\n    11\tThis guide covers essential PDF reading operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features (pypdfium2 rendering, pdfplumber table settings, OCR fallback, encrypted/corrupted PDF handling), see REFERENCE.md.\n    12\t\n    13\t## Reading & Inspecting PDFs\n    14\t\n    15\tBefore doing anything with a PDF, understand what you're working with.\n    16\t\n    17\t### Content inventory\n    18\t\n    19\tRun a quick diagnostic first. For simple tasks (\"summarize this\n    20\tdocument\"), `pdfinfo` + `pdffonts` + a text sample may suffice. For\n    21\tanything involving figures, attachments, or extraction issues, run the\n    22\tfull set:\n    23\t\n    24\t```bash\n    25\t# Always: page count, file size, PDF version, metadata\n    26\tpdfinfo document.pdf\n    27\t\n    28\t# Always: does a text layer exist? No fonts \u2192 scanned/raster \u2192 see \"Scanned documents\"\n    29\tpdffonts document.pdf\n    30\t\n    31\t# If fonts are present: sample the text layer\n    32\tpdftotext -f 1 -l 1 document.pdf - | head -20\n    33\t\n    34\t# If figures/charts may matter:\n    35\tpdfimages -list document.pdf\n    36\t\n    37\t# If the PDF might contain embedded files (reports, portfolios):\n    38\tpdfdetach -list document.pdf\n    39\t```\n    40\t\n    41\tThis tells you:\n    42\t- **Page count and size** \u2014 how big is the job?\n    43\t- **Font status** \u2014 are any fonts present? An empty `pdffonts` table\n    44\t  means the PDF is scanned or raster-only: `pdftotext` will return\n    45\t  nothing, so skip straight to \"Scanned documents\" below. Fonts shown\n    46\t  as not embedded (\"emb: no\") with custom encodings may produce wrong\n    47\t  characters on extraction.\n    48\t- **Text extractability** \u2014 when fonts exist, does `pdftotext` return\n    49\t  clean text, or is it garbled (broken encoding)?\n    50\t- **Embedded raster images** \u2014 are there photos or raster figures?\n    51\t  (Note: vector-drawn charts from matplotlib/Excel won't appear \u2014 see\n    52\t  \"Extracting embedded images\" below)\n    53\t- **Attachments** \u2014 are there embedded spreadsheets, data files, etc.?\n    54\t\n    55\t### Text extraction\n    56\t\n    57\t**pypdf** for basic text:\n    58\t```python\n    59\tfrom pypdf import PdfReader\n    60\t\n    61\treader = PdfReader(\"document.pdf\")\n    62\tprint(f\"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}\")\n    63\t\n    64\t# Extract text\n    65\ttext = \"\"\n    66\tfor page in reader.pages:\n    67\t    text += page.extract_text()\n    68\t```\n    69\t\n    70\t**pdftotext** preserving layout (better for multi-column docs):\n    71\t```bash\n    72\t# Layout mode preserves spatial positioning\n    73\tpdftotext -layout document.pdf output.txt\n    74\t\n    75\t# Specific page range\n    76\tpdftotext -f 1 -l 5 document.pdf output.txt\n    77\t```\n    78\t\n    79\t**pdfplumber** for layout-aware extraction with positioning data:\n    80\t```python\n    81\timport pdfplumber\n    82\t\n    83\twith pdfplumber.open(\"document.pdf\") as pdf:\n    84\t    for page in pdf.pages:\n    85\t        text = page.extract_text()\n    86\t        print(text)\n    87\t```\n    88\t\n    89\t### Visual inspection (rasterize pages)\n    90\t\n    91\tText extraction is **blind** to charts, diagrams, figures, equations,\n    92\tmulti-column layout, and form structures. When any of these matter,\n    93\trasterize the relevant page and Read the image:\n    94\t\n    95\t```bash\n    96\t# Rasterize a single page (page 3 here) at 150 DPI\n    97\tpdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f 3 -l 3 document.pdf /tmp/page\n    98\t\n    99\t# pdftoppm zero-pads the output filename based on TOTAL page count\n   100\t# (e.g., page-03.jpg for a 50-page PDF, page-003.jpg for 200+ pages)\n   101\t# Don't guess the filename \u2014 find it:\n   102\tls /tmp/page-*.jpg\n   103\t```\n   104\t\n   105\tThen Read the resulting image file. This gives you full visual\n   106\tunderstanding of that page \u2014 layout, charts, equations, everything.\n   107\t\n   108\t**When to rasterize vs. text-extract:**\n   109\t- **Content/data questions \u2192 text extraction** (cheaper, searchable)\n   110\t- **Figures, charts, visual layout \u2192 rasterize the page**\n   111\t- **Tables \u2192 try text extraction first, rasterize if garbled**\n   112\t- **Precision matters \u2192 do both** (extract text AND rasterize; use text\n   113\t  for data, image for context \u2014 this is what Claude's API does natively\n   114\t  with PDF uploads)\n   115\t\n   116\t**Token cost awareness:**\n   117\t- Text extraction: ~200\u2013400 tokens per page\n   118\t- Rasterized image: ~1,600 tokens per page (at 150 DPI)\n   119\t- Both together: ~2,000\u20132,400 tokens per page\n   120\t\n   121\tFor a 100-page PDF, rasterizing everything would consume ~160K tokens.\n   122\tOnly rasterize pages that matter for the question at hand.\n   123\t\n   124\t### Choosing your reading strategy\n   125\t\n   126\t**Text-heavy documents** (reports, articles, books):\n   127\t\u2192 Text extraction is primary. Rasterize only for specific figures or\n   128\t  pages where layout matters.\n   129\t\n   130\t**Scanned documents** (`pdffonts` shows no fonts):\n   131\t\u2192 `pdftotext` will return nothing \u2014 don't run it. Rasterize pages at\n   132\t  150 DPI and Read them visually. For bulk text extraction, use OCR\n   133\t  (pytesseract after converting pages to images \u2014 see REFERENCE.md for\n   134\t  a complete example).\n   135\t\n   136\t**Slide-deck PDFs** (exported presentations):\n   137\t\u2192 Every page is primarily visual. Rasterize individual pages on demand.\n   138\t  Text extraction gives you bullet-point text but loses all layout.\n   139\t\n   140\t**Form-heavy documents**:\n   141\t\u2192 Extract form field values programmatically first (see below). Rasterize\n   142\t  the form page for visual context if needed.\n   143\t\n   144\t**Data-heavy documents** (tables, charts, figures):\n   145\t\u2192 Use pdfplumber for tables. Rasterize pages with charts/figures.\n   146\t  Extract text for surrounding narrative. Consider both text AND image\n   147\t  for the same page when precision matters.\n   148\t\n   149\t### Extracting embedded images\n   150\t\n   151\t```bash\n   152\t# List all embedded images with metadata (size, color, compression)\n   153\tpdfimages -list document.pdf\n   154\t\n   155\t# Extract all images as PNG\n   156\tpdfimages -png document.pdf /tmp/img\n   157\t\n   158\t# Extract from specific pages only (pages 3-5)\n   159\tpdfimages -png -f 3 -l 5 document.pdf /tmp/img\n   160\t\n   161\t# Extract in original format (JPEG stays JPEG, etc.)\n   162\tpdfimages -all document.pdf /tmp/img\n   163\t```\n   164\t\n   165\tThen Read `/tmp/img-000.png` (etc.) to see each extracted image.\n   166\t\n   167\t**Gotcha \u2014 vector graphics:** `pdfimages` extracts only raster image\n   168\tdata. Charts and diagrams drawn as vector graphics (common in\n   169\tmatplotlib, Excel, and R exports) will NOT appear \u2014 they are page\n   170\tcontent operators, not image objects. For these, rasterize the whole\n   171\tpage with `pdftoppm` instead.\n   172\t\n   173\t**Gotcha \u2014 empty images:** `pdfimages` sometimes produces many tiny or\n   174\tempty image files \u2014 these are typically background masks, transparency\n   175\tlayers, or decorative elements. Filter by file size to find the real\n   176\tcontent images.\n   177\t\n   178\tProgrammatic extraction with position data:\n   179\t```python\n   180\timport fitz  # PyMuPDF\n   181\t\n   182\tdoc = fitz.open(\"document.pdf\")\n   183\tfor page in doc:\n   184\t    for img in page.get_images():\n   185\t        xref = img[0]\n   186\t        pix = fitz.Pixmap(doc, xref)\n   187\t        if pix.n - pix.alpha > 3:  # CMYK or other non-RGB\n   188\t            pix = fitz.Pixmap(fitz.csRGB, pix)\n   189\t        pix.save(f\"/tmp/img_{xref}.png\")\n   190\t```\n   191\t\n   192\t### Extracting file attachments\n   193\t\n   194\tPDFs can contain embedded files \u2014 spreadsheets, data files, other\n   195\tdocuments. Common in business reports, PDF portfolios, and PDF/A-3\n   196\tcompliance documents.\n   197\t\n   198\t```bash\n   199\t# List all attachments\n   200\tpdfdetach -list document.pdf\n   201\t\n   202\t# Extract all attachments to a directory\n   203\tmkdir -p /tmp/attachments\n   204\tpdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/attachments/ document.pdf\n   205\t\n   206\t# Extract a specific attachment by number (1-based index from -list output)\n   207\tpdfdetach -save 1 -o /tmp/attachment.pdf document.pdf\n   208\t```\n   209\t\n   210\tIn Python:\n   211\t```python\n   212\timport os\n   213\tfrom pypdf import PdfReader\n   214\t\n   215\treader = PdfReader(\"document.pdf\")\n   216\tfor name, content_list in reader.attachments.items():\n   217\t    safe_name = os.path.basename(name)  # sanitize \u2014 name comes from the PDF\n   218\t    for content in content_list:\n   219\t        with open(f\"/tmp/{safe_name}\", \"wb\") as f:\n   220\t            f.write(content)\n   221\t```\n   222\t\n   223\t**Two attachment mechanisms exist in PDFs:** page-level file annotation\n   224\tattachments (shown as paperclip icons in viewers) and document-level\n   225\tembedded files (in the EmbeddedFiles name tree). Both `pdfdetach` and\n   226\tpypdf handle the common cases. Rich media assets (3D, video) embedded\n   227\tas annotations may not appear in the attachment list \u2014 use PyMuPDF to\n   228\titerate page annotations for those.\n   229\t\n   230\t### Extracting form field data\n   231\t\n   232\tPDFs with interactive forms (government forms, applications, contracts)\n   233\thave fillable fields whose values can be read programmatically:\n   234\t\n   235\t```python\n   236\tfrom pypdf import PdfReader\n   237\t\n   238\treader = PdfReader(\"form.pdf\")\n   239\t\n   240\t# Text input fields only:\n   241\tfields = reader.get_form_text_fields()\n   242\tfor name, value in fields.items():\n   243\t    print(f\"{name}: {value}\")\n   244\t\n   245\t# All field types (checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns too):\n   246\tall_fields = reader.get_fields() or {}\n   247\tfor name, field in all_fields.items():\n   248\t    print(f\"{name}: {field.get('/V', '')} (type: {field.get('/FT', '')})\")\n   249\t```\n   250\t\n   251\t`get_form_text_fields()` returns only text input fields. For\n   252\tgovernment forms and contracts that use checkboxes, radio buttons,\n   253\tand dropdowns, use `get_fields()` instead to see all field types.\n   254\t\n   255\tFor comprehensive field info (types, options, defaults):\n   256\t```bash\n   257\tpdftk form.pdf dump_data_fields\n   258\t```\n   259\t\n   260\tFor anything beyond reading form data \u2014 filling forms, creating forms \u2014\n   261\tuse the `pdf` skill \u2014 invoke it by name if you have a Skill tool, or\n   262\tRead its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in the same\n   263\tskills directory as this file).\n   264\t\n   265\t### Audio, video, and other rare embedded content\n   266\t\n   267\tPDFs can occasionally embed audio, video, or 3D models. Check\n   268\t`pdfdetach -list` first \u2014 if the media appears as an attachment,\n   269\textract with `pdfdetach -saveall`. If not, it may be a Rich Media\n   270\tannotation (harder to extract; requires PyMuPDF to iterate page\n   271\tannotations). This is very rare in practice. Most PDF viewers outside\n   272\tAdobe Acrobat do not support media playback.\n   273\t\n   274\t### Font diagnostics\n   275\t\n   276\tIf text extraction produces garbled output (wrong characters, missing\n   277\ttext, mojibake), look back at the `pdffonts` output from the Content\n   278\tinventory. Check the \"emb\" column \u2014 fonts showing \"no\" (not embedded)\n   279\twith custom encodings mean the PDF's character mapping may be broken\n   280\tfor text extraction. In that case, rasterize the page and use vision\n   281\tinstead.\n   282\t\n   283\tAlso check encoding: fonts with \"Custom\" or \"Identity-H\" encoding\n   284\twithout embedded CIDToGID maps can cause character substitution issues\n   285\teven when the font is technically embedded.\n   286\t\n   287\t---\n   288\t\n   289\t## Quick Reference\n   290\t\n   291\t| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |\n   292\t|------|-----------|--------------|\n   293\t| Inspect PDF | poppler-utils | `pdfinfo`, `pdfimages -list`, `pdfdetach -list`, `pdffonts` |\n   294\t| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |\n   295\t| Extract text (CLI) | pdftotext | `pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt` |\n   296\t| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |\n   297\t| See page visually | pdftoppm | `pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f N -l N` |\n   298\t| Extract images | pdfimages | `pdfimages -png input.pdf prefix` |\n   299\t| Extract attachments | pdfdetach | `pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/` |\n   300\t| Read form fields | pypdf | `reader.get_fields()` |\n   301\t| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |\n   302\t\n   303\t## PDF Form Filling, Creation, Merging, Splitting, and Other Operations\n   304\t\n   305\tThis skill covers **reading and inspection** only. For filling forms,\n   306\tcreating, merging, splitting, rotating, watermarking, encrypting, or\n   307\tother PDF manipulation tasks, use the `pdf` skill (find its SKILL.md\n   308\tlocation in your available skills).\n   309\t",
                                "uuid": "698d6859-6204-432a-8c9c-1daba9e215ae"
                            }
                        ],

                            "path": "/home/claude/ocr.py",
                            "file_text": "import sys, subprocess\nfrom PIL import Image, ImageOps, ImageFilter\n\ndef ocr(path, lang=\"guj+eng\", psm=\"4\", scale=4):\n    im = Image.open(path).convert(\"L\")\n    im = im.resize((im.width*scale, im.height*scale), Image.LANCZOS)\n    im = ImageOps.autocontrast(im, cutoff=2)\n    im = im.filter(ImageFilter.SHARPEN)\n    tmp = \"/tmp/_ocr.png\"\n    im.save(tmp)\n    r = subprocess.run([\"tesseract\", tmp, \"-\", \"-l\", lang, \"--psm\", psm],\n                       capture_output=True, text=True)\n    return r.stdout\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    p = sys.argv[1]\n    lang = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else \"guj+eng\"\n    psm = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else \"4\"\n    out = ocr(p, lang, psm)\n    print(\"\\n\".join(l for l in out.splitlines() if l.strip()))\n"

                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "I dug into the documents properly, and I have to be straight with you before I build anything: I can't reliably read the trust's name or its objects clause, and I'm not willing to invent them for a page that goes public.\n\nHere's what happened, and one thing you should know regardless of the website.\n\n**Your files aren't PDFs.** All eight are ZIP archives full of JPEG photos, renamed with a `.pdf` extension \u2014 they came out of OKEN Scanner. They open fine in some viewers, which is why you haven't hit trouble yet, but they will be rejected by the Charity Commissioner's portal, the income tax portal, and Razorpay's KYC upload, all of which validate the actual file format rather than the name. Worth converting them to real PDFs before you need them under deadline.\n\n**What I could extract:**\n\n- **Trustees** \u2014 Hasmukhlal Keshavlal Vithlani (b. 17/10/1966, PAN ABOPV5280A), Sagunaben Hasmukhlal Vithlani (b. 18/12/1972), and Vishva Hasmukhbhai Vithlani (b. 19/09/2000). A three-member family trust.\n- **Location** \u2014 Dwarka taluka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, PIN 361335.\n- **Trust PAN** \u2014 AAZTS5070P, from the affidavit filename.\n- **Name shape** \u2014 the header reads as something like \"\u0ab6\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ac0 \u2026 \u0a9a\u0ac7\u0ab0\u0abf\u0a9f\u0ac7\u0aac\u0ab2 \u0a9f\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ab8\u0acd\u0a9f\", but the two or three distinguishing words in the middle come out as pure noise.\n\n**What defeated me:** the scans are 924\u00d71316, which is roughly a third of what Gujarati OCR needs. I installed the Gujarati language pack and ran the pages upscaled and contrast-corrected \u2014 the boilerplate legal text came through readable, but every line that matters (the name clause, the objects) is degraded exactly where the ink is densest. The objects clause hints at education, medical relief, and animal welfare, but \"hints at\" is doing far too much work in that sentence to put it on a website.\n\nI could guess. I'd rather not \u2014 a trust's stated mission on its own public page is the one thing that has to be exactly right, and a plausible-sounding invention is worse than a blank page.\n\n---\n\n**So, six things and I'll build it today:**\n\n1. Trust name, in Gujarati and English, exactly as registered\n2. Registration number and date, from the Charity Commissioner\n3. What the trust actually does \u2014 plain sentences, not the objects clause. Which people, what help, where.\n4. Contact email and phone for the site\n5. Full postal address as you want it shown publicly\n6. The domain you've bought\n\nIf the name and objects are easier to just retype from the physical deed than to re-scan, that's completely fine \u2014 a couple of lines typed out is faster than anything else here. Alternatively, re-photograph just the name clause and the objects pages in good light at full resolution and I'll pull them out myself.\n\nOne thing I'll say in advance, because it's already shaping how I'd approach this: **Dwarka is an unusually strong anchor.** A coastal temple town on the Gomti creek, one of the Char Dham, with a very particular light and palette \u2014 sandstone, sea, the flag over the Jagat Mandir. A trust rooted there has visual material available to it that a generic NGO in a generic city does not, and that's where I'd look for the signature element rather than reaching for the usual charity-sector green.\n\nTell me what the trust does, and I'll show you two directions.",

                    }
