                        "text": "Here's your page. One file, zero dependencies, zero JavaScript. Everything loads in a single request.\n\nA few things to note about what's in there and what you should change before deploying:\n\n**The favicon** is inline \u2014 a tiny SVG of the horizon concept itself (limestone sky, saffron line, sea below). It'll show in the browser tab and bookmarks. When you have a real logo later, replace it.\n\n**The saffron appears exactly once** \u2014 on \"Est. 2019 \u00b7 Dwarka.\" That restraint is deliberate. If you add more saffron later, the page stops feeling precise and starts feeling decorated.\n\n**The Gujarati name renders in the sea blue-grey**, not black. This creates a visual hierarchy \u2014 the English name is the architectural element (loud, tracked, uppercase), the Gujarati name is the quieter identity underneath it, and the colour tie to the horizon line connects them.\n\n**Three things you need to fill in before going live:**\n\nFirst, add `og:url` in the `<head>` once you know your domain \u2014 `<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://yourdomain.com\">`. Without it, WhatsApp previews work but some platforms won't deduplicate shares correctly.\n\nSecond, if you want a contact email or phone on the page, add it inside the `.meta` div \u2014 I left it out because you didn't provide one and publishing contact info is a decision, not a default.\n\nThird, verify the Gujarati name is character-perfect. I read it from the deed scans: **\u0ab8\u0acd\u0ab5. \u0aa6\u0ac7\u0ab5\u0a95\u0ac1\u0a82\u0ab5\u0ab0\u0aac\u0ac7\u0aa8 \u0a95\u0ac7\u0ab6\u0ab5\u0ab2\u0abe\u0ab2 \u0aad\u0abe\u0aa3\u0a9c\u0ac0 \u0ab5\u0abf\u0aa0\u0ab2\u0abe\u0aa3\u0ac0 \u0a9a\u0ac7\u0ab0\u0ac0\u0a9f\u0ac7\u0aac\u0ab2 \u0a9f\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ab8\u0acd\u0a9f** \u2014 but you should compare it against the physical copy, particularly the matras on \u0aa6\u0ac7\u0ab5\u0a95\u0ac1\u0a82\u0ab5\u0ab0\u0aac\u0ac7\u0aa8 and \u0ab5\u0abf\u0aa0\u0ab2\u0abe\u0aa3\u0ac0.\n\nTo deploy: drag this single file into a new Cloudflare Pages project, point your domain, done.",

                                "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: frontend-design\n     3\tdescription: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.\n     4\tlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# Frontend Design\n     8\t\n     9\tApproach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.\n    10\t\n    11\t## Ground it in the subject\n    12\t\n    13\tIf the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before \u2013 use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n    14\t\n    15\t## Design principles\n    16\t\n    17\tFor web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.\n    18\t\n    19\tTypography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n    20\t\n    21\tStructure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.\n    22\t\n    23\tLeverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.\n    24\t\n    25\tMatch complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.\n    26\t\n    27\tConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\n    28\t\n    29\t## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again\n    30\t\n    31\tFor calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 \u2014 Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell); (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly \u2014 the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\n    32\t\n    33\tWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4\u20136 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.\n    34\t\n    35\tThen review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief \u2014 revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.\n    36\t\n    37\tWhen writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.\n    38\t\n    39\tTry to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.\n    40\t\n    41\t## Restraint and self-critique\n    42\t\n    43\tSpend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it \u2013 a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.\n    44\t\n    45\t## More on writing in design\n    46\t\n    47\tWords appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.\n    48\t\n    49\tWrite from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.\n    50\t\n    51\tUse active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\n    52\t\n    53\tTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.\n    54\t\n    55\tKeep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.\n    56\t",

                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "Completely different page this time. Still one file, zero external dependencies, but now it's a proper website with structure.\n\nWhat's in it: a full-viewport hero with a deep coastal gradient and the SVG wave breaking into the content below, sticky navigation that goes translucent on scroll, an About section with the mission text and four highlight cards (25+ areas, 2019 founding, 12A, 80G), nine scope-of-work cards with inline SVG icons and hover effects, a trust details section with the PAN and registration info, and a proper footer. Everything scroll-animates into view using IntersectionObserver, and reduced-motion users get it all instantly without animation.\n\nTwo things I marked deliberately as \"Registration in process\" \u2014 the 12A and 80G cards. Once your lawyer hands those over, replace those with the actual registration numbers and dates. And the highlight cards currently show them as section labels; once confirmed, they become real proof points instead of placeholders.\n\nThe 12A/80G note matters for copy: I did **not** write \"tax-deductible donations available\" anywhere on the page, because until you've confirmed the effective date with your CA, that claim could mislead a donor. The cards say what the registrations are, not what benefit they promise. Swap the language once you're cleared.\n\nTell me what you think and what you'd change \u2014 colours, layout, copy, sections, anything. This is the version we iterate on.",
                        "citations": []
                    }

                "uuid": "019fb323-48e1-7057-b891-a993aaf2d5ac",
                "text": "Content wise it's okay but as we don't need SEO or ranking, can't we go for something visually and functinoally out of the box?",

            {
                "uuid": "019fb323-48e1-71b3-bc75-a95bdf286330",
                "text": "The user wants something visually and functionally \"out of the box\" - they want something truly impressive, interactive, and memorable. Since SEO doesn't matter, we can go full React/interactive with animations, 3D effects, parallax, creative interactions, etc.\n\nLet me think about what would genuinely impress:\n\n1. Interactive elements - maybe a canvas-based background with waves/particles\n2. Smooth parallax scrolling\n3. Creative page transitions\n4. Maybe a 3D element or WebGL effect\n5. Unique navigation concept\n6. Micro-interactions everywhere\n7. Creative typography animations\n8. A scroll-driven narrative that unfolds as the user moves down the page\n\nSince we don't need SEO, I can lean heavily into JavaScript and create something award-winning. I'm considering features like an animated ocean or wave canvas in the hero section, text that reveals with clip-path animations on scroll, cards with 3D tilt effects on hover, a custom cursor, smooth scrolling behavior, sections that transform as you scroll, animated counters, a loading animation, magnetic buttons, and text scramble effects. I'm thinking about what's actually achievable in a single HTML file while still looking genuinely impressive and unique - maybe something like \"The Living Coast\" as a concept.\n\nThe whole experience should feel alive and premium, with the ocean moving, text revealing itself, cards responding to the cursor, and smooth transitions between sections. I'm considering an animated canvas ocean with sine wave functions, scroll-triggered text reveals, magnetic cards with 3D perspective, smooth section transitions, a custom cursor that grows on hover, animated number counters, text scramble on the hero title, and a horizontal scroll section for cards. But I should probably narrow this down and not overdo it.\n\nI'm settling on the 4-5 most impactful effects: a canvas wave animation as the signature element, smooth scroll-triggered reveals with staggered timing, 3D tilt cards on hover, animated counters for stats, and smooth page-wide scroll with momentum. For typography, I'll load a beautiful display font for headings and a clean body font from Google Fonts since SEO isn't a concern. I'm debating whether to use Three.js for WebGL waves or stick with Canvas 2D for simplicity, and I'm leaning toward Canvas 2D. Now I'm building the canvas wave effect with layered sine waves at different amplitudes...\n\nBuilding the interactive effects...\n\nI'm structuring the page with a loading screen, hero section with the canvas wave background and animated text, an about section with parallax, stats with animated counters, scope cards with 3D tilt effects, and trust details. I'll add loading animations, parallax on scroll, a gradient that shifts based on scroll position, and hover effects throughout.\n\nFor the color palette, I'm going with a modern coastal theme\u2014deep navy to teal gradient with saffron gold accents and clean whites. I'll also include a hamburger menu for mobile with a full-screen overlay.\n\nThe file size should stay reasonable at around 15-20KB gzipped, which is totally acceptable for a single page. Now I'm ready to start building this out with careful structure and organization.\n\nI'm layering multiple wave animations on the canvas with different amplitudes, frequencies, and speeds to create depth, then adding features like 3D tilt effects on cards, animated counters, mobile menu toggle, smooth scrolling, and parallax effects.\n\nWriting canvas animation... Writing component code...\n\nThe real differentiator should be the interactive canvas waves in the hero section that respond to cursor movement\u2014the wave amplitude shifts where your mouse is, giving it that living, reactive quality. I could layer a parallax starfield above it for depth, but I should keep it focused. The core interactive pieces are the responsive canvas waves, the 3D tilt cards, and scroll-triggered animations that feel satisfying.\n\nFor typography, I want something that signals modern and premium without being generic. \"Sora\" or \"Manrope\" for headings would give it character while keeping the body text in system fonts for performance.\n\nActually, I'm overthinking this\u2014the design and interactions are what'll make it stand out, not the typeface choice. Let me stick with system fonts and focus on the visual treatment instead.\n\nNow I'm ready to start building. I'm thinking of a loading sequence where a saffron horizon line animates in from the center against a dark background, the trust initials fade in, then everything slides up to reveal the full site. But honestly, a loading screen might feel artificial on a static site\u2014maybe I should skip it and go straight into an orchestrated entrance animation instead.\n\nI'm planning a staggered fade-in sequence for the hero elements: the background gradient and canvas waves render immediately, then the \"Est. 2019\" badge fades in after 300ms, followed by the trust name at 500ms, the Gujarati text at 700ms, the tagline at 900ms, and finally the scroll indicator at 1200ms. This creates a cinematic feel without the fake loading screen.\n\nI'm also considering a more dramatic reveal where the hero isn't full-viewport\u2014instead, the page starts mostly black and as you scroll, the wave animation recedes to expose the content below.\n\nActually, that might be overcomplicating things. Instead, I'm thinking about making the scope cards section horizontally scrollable as you scroll down the page\u2014a scroll-jacking technique that feels premium but could be annoying if not executed smoothly. On mobile, I'd use CSS scroll-snap for a cleaner experience. But for a portfolio site, that might frustrate users, so I'm leaning toward keeping vertical scrolling and instead making the cards visually striking with 3D tilt and glow effects on hover.\n\nHere's my final feature set: canvas ocean waves with cursor interaction in the hero, orchestrated entrance animations, 3D tilt cards with glow, scroll-triggered reveals with stagger, animated counters, parallax scrolling on the hero, full-screen mobile nav overlay, sticky nav with blur backdrop, cursor-following gradient in the scope section, and smooth scrolling throughout. I'm also planning to enhance the footer with a callback to the wave effect or a matching gradient, and add a subtle grain texture overlay to the hero for that cinematic, premium feel.\n\nWriting SVG filter code...\n\nNow I'm refining the color palette to match that coastal, sea-inspired direction the user preferred\u2014keeping the DNA but making it more vibrant and modern with deep navy backgrounds, sea-toned accents, and lighter sea highlights for contrast.Since SEO doesn't matter, we can throw out all the static-HTML constraints and go fully interactive. Canvas, 3D, cursor-reactive, animated \u2014 the kind of thing that makes someone pause and say \"wait, this is a placeholder?\"\n\nThis will take me a minute. Building it properly.\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nCompletely different animal from the last one. Still one file, still zero dependencies, but now it's interactive and alive.\n\nWhat's actually happening under the hood:\n\n**The hero ocean** is a real-time Canvas 2D animation \u2014 four layered sine waves with different amplitudes, frequencies, and speeds, composited with transparency. They respond to your cursor: move your mouse across the hero and the waves swell gently where you are. There's also a soft radial glow that follows your cursor, like light catching the water surface.\n\n**The 3D tilt cards** in the scope section respond to your mouse position with perspective transforms \u2014 they physically tilt toward your cursor and spring back when you leave. Each card also has a cursor-following highlight glow underneath.\n\n**The entrance** is orchestrated \u2014 the badge, title, subtitle, and tagline cascade in with staggered timing on a custom cubic-bezier curve, rather than everything appearing at once.\n\n**Parallax** on the hero content: as you scroll down, the text drifts upward and fades, while the wave canvas stays anchored. The sticky nav transitions from transparent to frosted-glass with backdrop-filter blur.\n\n**Counters** animate up when they scroll into view \u2014 the \"25+\" and \"2019\" count up with an ease-out curve.\n\n**Film grain** \u2014 a subtle SVG fractalNoise filter overlaid at 3% opacity. Barely visible, but it adds a textured, almost cinematic quality that separates it from the flat digital look.\n\nEverything respects `prefers-reduced-motion` \u2014 users who've set that preference get a completely static page with no animation, no parallax, no tilt. The mobile version has a full-screen nav overlay with animated hamburger.\n\nOpen it in a proper browser to see the full effect \u2014 the canvas waves and cursor interactions won't show in the preview here. How does this land?",

Devkunvarben Kesavlal Bhanaji Vithalani Charitable Trust</p>\n        <p class=\"footer-gu\" lang=\"gu\">\u0ab8\u0acd\u0ab5. \u0aa6\u0ac7\u0ab5\u0a95\u0ac1\u0a82\u0ab5\u0ab0\u0aac\u0ac7\u0aa8 \u0a95\u0ac7\u0ab6\u0ab5\u0ab2\u0abe\u0ab2 \u0aad\u0abe\u0aa3\u0a9c\u0ac0 \u0ab5\u0abf\u0aa0\u0ab2\u0abe\u0aa3\u0ac0 \u0a9a\u0ac7\u0ab0\u0ac0\u0a9f\u0ac7\u0aac\u0ab2 \u0a9f\u0acd\u0ab0\u0ab8\u0acd\u0a9f</p>\n        <div class=\"footer-divider\"></div>\n        <p class=\"footer-status\">Full website under development</p>\n        <p class=\"footer-copy\">&copy; 2026 SDKBV Charitable Trust. All rights reserved.</p>\n    </footer>\n\n    <script>\n    (function() {\n        'use strict';\n\n        // ===== CANVAS OCEAN WAVES =====\n        const canvas = document.getElementById('waveCanvas');\n        const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');\n        let W, H, mouseX = 0.5, mouseY = 0.5, time = 0;\n        const prefersReduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;\n\n        function resizeCanvas() {\n            const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2);\n            const rect = canvas.parentElement.getBoundingClientRect();\n            W = rect.width;\n            H = rect.height;\n            canvas.width = W * dpr;\n            canvas.height = H * dpr;\n            canvas.style.width = W + 'px';\n            canvas.style.height = H + 'px';\n            ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);\n        }\n        resizeCanvas();\n        window.addEventListener('resize', resizeCanvas);\n\n        const waves = [\n            { y: 0.68, amp: 28, freq: 0.004, speed: 0.008, color: 'rgba(26, 75, 110, 0.18)' },\n            { y: 0.72, amp: 22, freq: 0.006, speed: 0.012, color: 'rgba(42, 124, 165, 0.12)' },\n            { y: 0.76, amp: 16, freq: 0.008, speed: 0.006, color: 'rgba(19, 43, 68, 0.20)' },\n            { y: 0.80, amp: 12, freq: 0.010, speed: 0.015, color: 'rgba(212, 149, 43, 0.05)' },\n        ];\n\n        function drawWaves() {\n            ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);\n            waves.forEach(wave => {\n                ctx.beginPath();\n                ctx.moveTo(0, H);\n                for (let x = 0; x <= W; x += 3) {\n                    const mouseInfluence = Math.exp(-Math.pow((x / W - mouseX) * 3, 2)) * 8;\n                    const y = H * wave.y\n                        + Math.sin(x * wave.freq + time * wave.speed) * (wave.amp + mouseInfluence)\n                        + Math.sin(x * wave.freq * 0.4 + time * wave.speed * 1.7) * wave.amp * 0.4\n                        + Math.cos(x * wave.freq * 0.7 + time * wave.speed * 0.5) * wave.amp * 0.2;\n                    ctx.lineTo(x, y);\n                }\n                ctx.lineTo(W, H);\n                ctx.closePath();\n                ctx.fillStyle = wave.color;\n                ctx.fill();\n            });\n        }\n\n        function animate() {\n            time++;\n            drawWaves();\n            if (!prefersReduced) requestAnimationFrame(animate);\n        }\n        if (!prefersReduced) {\n            animate();\n        } else {\n            time = 100;\n            drawWaves();\n        }\n\n        // ===== HERO CURSOR GLOW =====\n        const heroGlow = document.getElementById('heroGlow');\n        const hero = document.querySelector('.hero');\n\n        hero.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {\n            const rect = hero.getBoundingClientRect();\n            const x = e.clientX - rect.left;\n            const y = e.clientY - rect.top;\n            mouseX = x / rect.width;\n            mouseY = y / rect.height;\n            heroGlow.style.transform = `translate(${x - 300}px, ${y - 300}px)`;\n        });\n\n        // ===== HERO ENTRANCE =====\n        setTimeout(() => {\n            document.querySelectorAll('.hero-anim').forEach(el => el.classList.add('entered'));\n        }, 200);\n\n        // ===== HERO PARALLAX ON SCROLL =====\n        const heroContent = document.querySelector('.hero-content');\n        window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {\n            const scrollY = window.scrollY;\n            if (scrollY < window.innerHeight && !prefersReduced) {\n                heroContent.style.transform = `translateY(${scrollY * 0.25}px)`;\n                heroContent.style.opacity = 1 - scrollY / (window.innerHeight * 0.8);\n            }\n        }, { passive: true });\n\n        // ===== NAV SCROLL =====\n        const nav = document.getElementById('nav');\n        const navObs = new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => {\n            nav.classList.toggle('scrolled', !e.isIntersecting);\n        }, { threshold: 0.05 });\n        navObs.observe(hero);\n\n        // ===== SCROLL REVEAL =====\n        const reveals = document.querySelectorAll('.reveal');\n        const revealObs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {\n            entries.forEach(entry => {\n                if (entry.isIntersecting) {\n                    entry.target.classList.add('visible');\n                    revealObs.unobserve(entry.target);\n                }\n            });\n        }, { threshold: 0.12, rootMargin: '0px 0px -30px 0px' });\n        reveals.forEach(el => revealObs.observe(el));\n\n        // ===== 3D TILT CARDS =====\n        if (!prefersReduced && window.innerWidth > 768) {\n            document.querySelectorAll('[data-tilt]').forEach(card => {\n                const glow = card.querySelector('.card-glow');\n\n                card.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {\n                    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();\n                    const x = e.clientX - rect.left;\n                    const y = e.clientY - rect.top;\n                    const cx = rect.width / 2;\n                    const cy = rect.height / 2;\n                    const rotX = ((y - cy) / cy) * -6;\n                    const rotY = ((x - cx) / cx) * 6;\n                    card.style.transform = `perspective(800px) rotateX(${rotX}deg) rotateY(${rotY}deg) scale(1.02)`;\n                    if (glow) {\n                        glow.style.left = x + 'px';\n                        glow.style.top = y + 'px';\n                    }\n                });\n\n                card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => {\n                    card.style.transform = 'perspective(800px) rotateX(0) rotateY(0) scale(1)';\n                    card.style.transition = 'transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)';\n                    setTimeout(() => { card.style.transition = ''; }, 500);\n                });\n            });\n        }\n\n        // ===== ANIMATED COUNTERS =====\n        const counters = document.querySelectorAll('[data-count]');\n        const counterObs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {\n            entries.forEach(entry => {\n                if (entry.isIntersecting) {\n                    const el = entry.target;\n                    const target = parseInt(el.dataset.count);\n                    const duration = target > 100 ? 1800 : 1200;\n                    const start = performance.now();\n                    const tick = (now) => {\n                        const p = Math.min((now - start) / duration, 1);\n                        const ease = 1 - Math.pow(1 - p, 4);\n                        el.textContent = Math.floor(ease * target);\n                        if (p < 1) requestAnimationFrame(tick);\n                    };\n                    requestAnimationFrame(tick);\n                    counterObs.unobserve(el);\n                }\n            });\n        }, { threshold: 0.5 });\n        counters.forEach(el => counterObs.observe(el));\n\n        // ===== MOBILE MENU =====\n        const menuBtn = document.getElementById('menuBtn');\n        const mobileNav = document.getElementById('mobileNav');\n        menuBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {\n            menuBtn.classList.toggle('active');\n            mobileNav.classList.toggle('open');\n            document.body.style.overflow = mobileNav.classList.contains('open') ? 'hidden' : '';\n        });\n        mobileNav.querySelectorAll('a').forEach(link => {\n            link.addEventListener('click', () => {\n                menuBtn.classList.remove('active');\n                mobileNav.classList.remove('open');\n                document.body.style.overflow = '';\n            });\n        });\n\n        // ===== SMOOTH SCROLL =====\n        document.querySelectorAll('a[href^=\"#\"]').forEach(link => {\n            link.addEventListener('click', (e) => {\n                e.preventDefault();\n                const target = document.querySelector(link.getAttribute('href'));\n                if (target) {\n                    const offset = 68;\n                    const y = target.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - offset;\n                    window.scrollTo({ top: y, behavior: 'smooth' });\n                }\n            });\n        });\n\n    })();\n    </script>\n</body>\n</html>\n",

                        },

All rights reserved.</p>\\n    </footer>\\n\\n    <script>\\n    (function() {\\n        'use strict';\\n\\n        // ===== CANVAS OCEAN WAVES =====\\n        const canvas = document.getElementById('waveCanvas');\\n        const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');\\n        let W, H, mouseX = 0.5, mouseY = 0.5, time = 0;\\n        const prefersReduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;\\n\\n        function resizeCanvas() {\\n            const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2);\\n            const rect = canvas.parentElement.getBoundingClientRect();\\n            W = rect.width;\\n            H = rect.height;\\n            canvas.width = W * dpr;\\n            canvas.height = H * dpr;\\n            canvas.style.width = W + 'px';\\n            canvas.style.height = H + 'px';\\n            ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);\\n        }\\n        resizeCanvas();\\n        window.addEventListener('resize', resizeCanvas);\\n\\n        const waves = [\\n            { y: 0.68, amp: 28, freq: 0.004, speed: 0.008, color: 'rgba(26, 75, 110, 0.18)' },\\n            { y: 0.72, amp: 22, freq: 0.006, speed: 0.012, color: 'rgba(42, 124, 165, 0.12)' },\\n            { y: 0.76, amp: 16, freq: 0.008, speed: 0.006, color: 'rgba(19, 43, 68, 0.20)' },\\n            { y: 0.80, amp: 12, freq: 0.010, speed: 0.015, color: 'rgba(212, 149, 43, 0.05)' },\\n        ];\\n\\n        function drawWaves() {\\n            ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);\\n            waves.forEach(wave => {\\n                ctx.beginPath();\\n                ctx.moveTo(0, H);\\n                for (let x = 0; x <= W; x += 3) {\\n                    const mouseInfluence = Math.exp(-Math.pow((x / W - mouseX) * 3, 2)) * 8;\\n                    const y = H * wave.y\\n                        + Math.sin(x * wave.freq + time * wave.speed) * (wave.amp + mouseInfluence)\\n                        + Math.sin(x * wave.freq * 0.4 + time * wave.speed * 1.7) * wave.amp * 0.4\\n                        + Math.cos(x * wave.freq * 0.7 + time * wave.speed * 0.5) * wave.amp * 0.2;\\n                    ctx.lineTo(x, y);\\n                }\\n                ctx.lineTo(W, H);\\n                ctx.closePath();\\n                ctx.fillStyle = wave.color;\\n                ctx.fill();\\n            });\\n        }\\n\\n        function animate() {\\n            time++;\\n            drawWaves();\\n            if (!prefersReduced) requestAnimationFrame(animate);\\n        }\\n        if (!prefersReduced) {\\n            animate();\\n        } else {\\n            time = 100;\\n            drawWaves();\\n        }\\n\\n        // ===== HERO CURSOR GLOW =====\\n        const heroGlow = document.getElementById('heroGlow');\\n        const hero = document.querySelector('.hero');\\n\\n        hero.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {\\n            const rect = hero.getBoundingClientRect();\\n            const x = e.clientX - rect.left;\\n            const y = e.clientY - rect.top;\\n            mouseX = x / rect.width;\\n            mouseY = y / rect.height;\\n            heroGlow.style.transform = `translate(${x - 300}px, ${y - 300}px)`;\\n        });\\n\\n        // ===== HERO ENTRANCE =====\\n        setTimeout(() => {\\n            document.querySelectorAll('.hero-anim').forEach(el => el.classList.add('entered'));\\n        }, 200);\\n\\n        // ===== HERO PARALLAX ON SCROLL =====\\n        const heroContent = document.querySelector('.hero-content');\\n        window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {\\n            const scrollY = window.scrollY;\\n            if (scrollY < window.innerHeight && !prefersReduced) {\\n                heroContent.style.transform = `translateY(${scrollY * 0.25}px)`;\\n                heroContent.style.opacity = 1 - scrollY / (window.innerHeight * 0.8);\\n            }\\n        }, { passive: true });\\n\\n        // ===== NAV SCROLL =====\\n        const nav = document.getElementById('nav');\\n        const navObs = new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => {\\n            nav.classList.toggle('scrolled', !e.isIntersecting);\\n        }, { threshold: 0.05 });\\n        navObs.observe(hero);\\n\\n        // ===== SCROLL REVEAL =====\\n        const reveals = document.querySelectorAll('.reveal');\\n        const revealObs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {\\n            entries.forEach(entry => {\\n                if (entry.isIntersecting) {\\n                    entry.target.classList.add('visible');\\n                    revealObs.unobserve(entry.target);\\n                }\\n            });\\n        }, { threshold: 0.12, rootMargin: '0px 0px -30px 0px' });\\n        reveals.forEach(el => revealObs.observe(el));\\n\\n        // ===== 3D TILT CARDS =====\\n        if (!prefersReduced && window.innerWidth > 768) {\\n            document.querySelectorAll('[data-tilt]').forEach(card => {\\n                const glow = card.querySelector('.card-glow');\\n\\n                card.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {\\n                    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();\\n                    const x = e.clientX - rect.left;\\n                    const y = e.clientY - rect.top;\\n                    const cx = rect.width / 2;\\n                    const cy = rect.height / 2;\\n                    const rotX = ((y - cy) / cy) * -6;\\n                    const rotY = ((x - cx) / cx) * 6;\\n                    card.style.transform = `perspective(800px) rotateX(${rotX}deg) rotateY(${rotY}deg) scale(1.02)`;\\n                    if (glow) {\\n                        glow.style.left = x + 'px';\\n                        glow.style.top = y + 'px';\\n                    }\\n                });\\n\\n                card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => {\\n                    card.style.transform = 'perspective(800px) rotateX(0) rotateY(0) scale(1)';\\n                    card.style.transition = 'transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)';\\n                    setTimeout(() => { card.style.transition = ''; }, 500);\\n                });\\n            });\\n        }\\n\\n        // ===== ANIMATED COUNTERS =====\\n        const counters = document.querySelectorAll('[data-count]');\\n        const counterObs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {\\n            entries.forEach(entry => {\\n                if (entry.isIntersecting) {\\n                    const el = entry.target;\\n                    const target = parseInt(el.dataset.count);\\n                    const duration = target > 100 ? 1800 : 1200;\\n                    const start = performance.now();\\n                    const tick = (now) => {\\n                        const p = Math.min((now - start) / duration, 1);\\n                        const ease = 1 - Math.pow(1 - p, 4);\\n                        el.textContent = Math.floor(ease * target);\\n                        if (p < 1) requestAnimationFrame(tick);\\n                    };\\n                    requestAnimationFrame(tick);\\n                    counterObs.unobserve(el);\\n                }\\n            });\\n        }, { threshold: 0.5 });\\n        counters.forEach(el => counterObs.observe(el));\\n\\n        // ===== MOBILE MENU =====\\n        const menuBtn = document.getElementById('menuBtn');\\n        const mobileNav = document.getElementById('mobileNav');\\n        menuBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {\\n            menuBtn.classList.toggle('active');\\n            mobileNav.classList.toggle('open');\\n            document.body.style.overflow = mobileNav.classList.contains('open') ? 'hidden' : '';\\n        });\\n        mobileNav.querySelectorAll('a').forEach(link => {\\n            link.addEventListener('click', () => {\\n                menuBtn.classList.remove('active');\\n                mobileNav.classList.remove('open');\\n                document.body.style.overflow = '';\\n            });\\n        });\\n\\n        // ===== SMOOTH SCROLL =====\\n        document.querySelectorAll('a[href^=\\\"#\\\"]').forEach(link => {\\n            link.addEventListener('click', (e) => {\\n                e.preventDefault();\\n                const target = document.querySelector(link.getAttribute('href'));\\n                if (target) {\\n                    const offset = 68;\\n                    const y = target.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - offset;\\n                    window.scrollTo({ top: y, behavior: 'smooth' });\\n                }\\n            });\\n        });\\n\\n    })();\\n    </script>\\n</body>\\n</html>\\n\", \"filename\": \"/mnt/user-data/outputs/index.html\"}"

                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "Completely different animal from the last one. Still one file, still zero dependencies, but now it's interactive and alive.\n\nWhat's actually happening under the hood:\n\n**The hero ocean** is a real-time Canvas 2D animation \u2014 four layered sine waves with different amplitudes, frequencies, and speeds, composited with transparency. They respond to your cursor: move your mouse across the hero and the waves swell gently where you are. There's also a soft radial glow that follows your cursor, like light catching the water surface.\n\n**The 3D tilt cards** in the scope section respond to your mouse position with perspective transforms \u2014 they physically tilt toward your cursor and spring back when you leave. Each card also has a cursor-following highlight glow underneath.\n\n**The entrance** is orchestrated \u2014 the badge, title, subtitle, and tagline cascade in with staggered timing on a custom cubic-bezier curve, rather than everything appearing at once.\n\n**Parallax** on the hero content: as you scroll down, the text drifts upward and fades, while the wave canvas stays anchored. The sticky nav transitions from transparent to frosted-glass with backdrop-filter blur.\n\n**Counters** animate up when they scroll into view \u2014 the \"25+\" and \"2019\" count up with an ease-out curve.\n\n**Film grain** \u2014 a subtle SVG fractalNoise filter overlaid at 3% opacity. Barely visible, but it adds a textured, almost cinematic quality that separates it from the flat digital look.\n\nEverything respects `prefers-reduced-motion` \u2014 users who've set that preference get a completely static page with no animation, no parallax, no tilt. The mobile version has a full-screen nav overlay with animated hamburger.\n\nOpen it in a proper browser to see the full effect \u2014 the canvas waves and cursor interactions won't show in the preview here. How does this land?",

                "uuid": "019fb820-29e7-7e1e-b348-7768b447c459",
                "text": "Hey research for me that what type of prompt is the correct for google ai studio. And also what technology can it develop the website in?",
                "content": [
                    {
                        "start_timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:22:25.448113Z",
                        "stop_timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:22:25.448113Z",
                        "flags": null,
                        "type": "text",

                        "citations": []

                ],
                "sender": "human",
                "created_at": "2026-07-31T12:22:25.448270Z",
                "updated_at": "2026-07-31T12:22:25.448270Z",

            {
                "uuid": "019fb820-29e7-7446-85b6-1df392e1bd34",
                "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nHere's a full breakdown of what you need to know about Google AI Studio \u2014 prompt types and web development capabilities:\n\n---\n\n## \ud83e\udde0 Prompt Types in Google AI Studio\n\nA prompt in Google AI Studio is a layered sequence that guides the Gemini model from context to action. Google divides this into five clear components:\n\n1. **System Instructions** \u2014 Define the model's role, tone, and constraints\n2. **User Context** \u2014 Describes the current data, problem, or question\n3. **Examples (Few-Shot Prompting)** \u2014 Demonstrate the expected input/output pattern\n4. **Task Instruction** \u2014 The direct goal or command\n5. **Output Specification** \u2014 Defines how results should be structured or formatted\n\n### The Main Prompt Modes:\n\n**Chat Prompts** \u2014 Used to build conversational experiences, this technique allows for multiple input and response turns to generate output. Other options include Realtime streaming, Video gen, and more.\n\n**Zero-Shot Prompting** \u2014 Write a baseline prompt in plain language and run it once as zero-shot prompting, saving the output as your control.\n\n**Few-Shot Prompting** \u2014 Models like Gemini can often pick up on patterns using a few examples, though you may need to experiment with the number of examples for best results. If you include too many examples, the model may start to overfit the response.\n\n**System Instructions** \u2014 Unlike standard prompts, these are high-priority, persistent constraints used to establish permanent personas, mandatory formatting, or a localized knowledge base for the entire session.\n\n**Structured / Build Mode Prompts** \u2014 For those looking to define structured task requirements, Build mode is the ideal environment to start your work.\n\n---\n\n## \ud83c\udf10 Website Development Technologies in Google AI Studio\n\nGoogle AI Studio supports building web apps with full-stack runtimes and native Android apps with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose \u2014 all through natural language prompting in Build mode.\n\nFor **web development** specifically:\n\n- **React / Next.js** \u2014 Google AI Studio has shifted from a mere playground to a sophisticated tool capable of scaffolding entire React or Next.js applications in minutes.\n\n- **Android Apps (Kotlin + Jetpack Compose)** \u2014 Google announced native Android app generation directly inside the browser at Google I/O 2026. Generated applications use Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, which are official Android development technologies. Apps can access GPS, Bluetooth, cameras, sensors, background services and offline features.\n\n- **Firebase Integration** \u2014 Firebase integrations such as Firestore, Firebase Auth, and Firebase App Check are on Google's roadmap, building on the earlier Firebase AI Logic and Stitch rollout.\n\n- **GitHub Export & Android Studio handoff** \u2014 AI Studio can hand projects to Android Studio through a ZIP download or GitHub export, extending the browser-based development path.\n\n---\n\n### \u2705 Quick Summary\n\n| Category | Details |\n|---|---|\n| **Prompt Types** | Chat, Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, System Instructions, Build Mode |\n| **Web Tech** | React, Next.js, full-stack runtimes |\n| **Mobile Tech** | Kotlin, Jetpack Compose (Android) |\n| **Backend/Cloud** | Firebase (Firestore, Auth), Google Maps, Gemini API |\n| **Export** | GitHub, ZIP, Android Studio, Google Play |\n\nGoogle AI Studio is essentially evolving into a full browser-based development platform \u2014 you can go from a text prompt to a deployable web or mobile app without leaving the browser.",

                                "text": "Unlock the full potential of Google AI Studio website development. Learn how to generate React code, manage API keys, and deploy live AI-powered apps.\n\nMay 10, 2026 \u00b7 Technical Tutorials, Automation Tools and Technologies \u00b7 If you think Google AI Studio is just a sandbox for testing prompts, you are missing out on one of the most powerful code-generation engines available today. It has shifted from a mere playground to a sophisticated tool capable of scaffolding entire React or Next.js applications in minutes. In this guide, I will walk you through how I use Google AI Studio to accelerate web development, identify the technical \u201cblind spots\u201d that most tutorials ignore, and show you how to move from a prompt to a live, production-ready website with automated deployment. \n\nMost AI website builders are \u201cblack boxes\u201d\u2014you give them a prompt, and they give you a static page you can barely customize.\n\n\n\nTechnologies in Physical Security (7) Bengali Pioneers of Indian Science: The 9 Architects of a Nation \u00b7 AI in Access Control Systems: Beyond the Basics \u00b7 How to Track YouTube Tutorials You Watch and Turn Them Into Actionable Notes \u00b7 How to Connect Gemini CLI to WordPress Using MCP \u00b7 How I Optimized 40 WordPress Posts to Perfect SEO Scores Using Gemini CLI SEO audit \u00b7 Archives \u00b7 Select Week \u00b7 May 17, 2026\u2013May 23, 2026 \u00b7 May 10, 2026\u2013May 16, 2026 \u00b7 February 1, 2026\u2013February 7, 2026 \u00b7 December 21, 2025\u2013December 27, 2025 \u00b7 December 14, 2025\u2013December 20, 2025 \u00b7 December 7, 2025\u2013December 13, 2025 \u00b7 November 30, 2025\u2013December 6, 2025 \u00b7 March 23, 2025\u2013March 29, 2025 \u00b7 December 22, 2024\u2013December 28, 2024 \u00b7 September 1, 2024\u2013September 7, 2024 \u00b7 August 25, 2024\u2013August 31, 2024 \u00b7 August 11, 2024\u2013August 17, 2024 \u00b7 July 7, 2024\u2013July 13, 2024 \u00b7\n\n\"The technology you use impresses no one.",

                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "Here's a full breakdown of what you need to know about Google AI Studio \u2014 prompt types and web development capabilities:\n\n---\n\n## \ud83e\udde0 Prompt Types in Google AI Studio\n\nA prompt in Google AI Studio is a layered sequence that guides the Gemini model from context to action. Google divides this into five clear components:\n\n1. **System Instructions** \u2014 Define the model's role, tone, and constraints\n2. **User Context** \u2014 Describes the current data, problem, or question\n3. **Examples (Few-Shot Prompting)** \u2014 Demonstrate the expected input/output pattern\n4. **Task Instruction** \u2014 The direct goal or command\n5. **Output Specification** \u2014 Defines how results should be structured or formatted\n\n### The Main Prompt Modes:\n\n**Chat Prompts** \u2014 Used to build conversational experiences, this technique allows for multiple input and response turns to generate output. Other options include Realtime streaming, Video gen, and more.\n\n**Zero-Shot Prompting** \u2014 Write a baseline prompt in plain language and run it once as zero-shot prompting, saving the output as your control.\n\n**Few-Shot Prompting** \u2014 Models like Gemini can often pick up on patterns using a few examples, though you may need to experiment with the number of examples for best results. If you include too many examples, the model may start to overfit the response.\n\n**System Instructions** \u2014 Unlike standard prompts, these are high-priority, persistent constraints used to establish permanent personas, mandatory formatting, or a localized knowledge base for the entire session.\n\n**Structured / Build Mode Prompts** \u2014 For those looking to define structured task requirements, Build mode is the ideal environment to start your work.\n\n---\n\n## \ud83c\udf10 Website Development Technologies in Google AI Studio\n\nGoogle AI Studio supports building web apps with full-stack runtimes and native Android apps with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose \u2014 all through natural language prompting in Build mode.\n\nFor **web development** specifically:\n\n- **React / Next.js** \u2014 Google AI Studio has shifted from a mere playground to a sophisticated tool capable of scaffolding entire React or Next.js applications in minutes.\n\n- **Android Apps (Kotlin + Jetpack Compose)** \u2014 Google announced native Android app generation directly inside the browser at Google I/O 2026. Generated applications use Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, which are official Android development technologies. Apps can access GPS, Bluetooth, cameras, sensors, background services and offline features.\n\n- **Firebase Integration** \u2014 Firebase integrations such as Firestore, Firebase Auth, and Firebase App Check are on Google's roadmap, building on the earlier Firebase AI Logic and Stitch rollout.\n\n- **GitHub Export & Android Studio handoff** \u2014 AI Studio can hand projects to Android Studio through a ZIP download or GitHub export, extending the browser-based development path.\n\n---\n\n### \u2705 Quick Summary\n\n| Category | Details |\n|---|---|\n| **Prompt Types** | Chat, Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, System Instructions, Build Mode |\n| **Web Tech** | React, Next.js, full-stack runtimes |\n| **Mobile Tech** | Kotlin, Jetpack Compose (Android) |\n| **Backend/Cloud** | Firebase (Firestore, Auth), Google Maps, Gemini API |\n| **Export** | GitHub, ZIP, Android Studio, Google Play |\n\nGoogle AI Studio is essentially evolving into a full browser-based development platform \u2014 you can go from a text prompt to a deployable web or mobile app without leaving the browser.",

Your Full Stack:\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Frontend | Angular 18+ with Angular Material |\n| Backend | Node.js + Express / NestJS |\n| Database | MongoDB Atlas (yours) |\n| Auth | JWT + Refresh Tokens + OAuth2 |\n| Live Video | WebRTC + Socket.io |\n| Recording | MediaRecorder API \u2192 encrypted S3/GCS |\n| Access Control | Casbin (supports RBAC+ABAC+ReBAC) |\n| Audit Trail | MongoDB Change Streams |\n\n---\n\n## \ud83d\udccb Your Google AI Studio Custom Instructions\n\nCopy this exactly into the **\"Custom instructions\"** tab in AI Studio:\n\n---\n\n```\n## PROJECT IDENTITY\nYou are building a private, enterprise-grade KYC Verification & Admin Management Platform. storage\n- Access Control Engine: Casbin with MongoDB adapter (supports RBAC + ABAC + ReBAC + PBAC)\n- Audit Trail: MongoDB Change Streams + custom AuditLog collection (immutable, append-only)\n\n## ACCESS CONTROL RULES\n- Implement a 4-layer hybrid policy engine: ReBAC (core) + ABAC (conditions) + RBAC (role buckets) + PBAC (policy sets)\n- The Super Admin role (me) has unrestricted access to ALL resources and can NEVER be locked out\n- All roles, permissions, conditions, and relationships must be manageable via a NO-CODE admin UI panel\n- The system must scale to 500-600 role types with thousands of users per role\n- Never hardcode permissions in the codebase \u2014 all policies must be stored in MongoDB and loaded dynamically\n- Every permission change must be logged in the AuditLog with: who changed it, what was changed, before/after state, timestamp\n\n## KYC VERIFICATION SYSTEM\n- Users submit verification via live camera + microphone (WebRTC stream)\n- Admin watches live in real-time AND session is simultaneously recorded\n- Location data (GPS coordinates) must be captured with user consent prompt\n- Every KYC session must have: sessionId, userId, startTime, endTime, recordingUrl (encrypted), locationData, auditTrail[], status (pending/approved/rejected/flagged)\n- Recordings must be encrypted before storage and only decryptable by users with explicit 'kyc.recording.view' permission\n- All KYC actions (start, pause, approve, reject, flag) must be logged immutably\n\n## SECURITY \u2014 NON-NEGOTIABLE\n- All API routes must have authentication middleware by default \u2014 no public routes unless explicitly marked @Public()\n- Implement rate limiting on all endpoints (especially auth and KYC endpoints)\n- Input validation on every DTO using class-validator\n- CORS locked to specific allowed origins only\n- Helmet.js for HTTP security headers\n- All sensitive data fields in MongoDB must be encrypted at rest (use mongoose-encryption or field-level encryption)\n- Never log passwords, tokens, or PII in console or log files\n- Implement CSRF protection for all state-changing operations\n\n## CODE STYLE & ARCHITECTURE\n- Use NestJS modular structure: each feature is its own module (auth, users, kyc, roles, permissions, audit)\n- Angular: use standalone components, lazy-loaded routes per feature module, strict TypeScript\n- localStorage for storing tokens (use httpOnly cookies only)\n- Never skip input validation\n- Never generate placeholder/mock data for security-critical features \u2014 implement it properly\n- Never suggest skipping encryption \"for now\" or \"in production\"\n- Never create public API endpoints without explicit instruction from me\n- Do not ask me about tech stack choices \u2014 the stack above is final\n\n## RESPONSE FORMAT\n- Always generate complete, production-ready code \u2014 no pseudo-code or \"you can add X here\"\n- When generating a new feature, output in this order: Schema \u2192 unnecessary explanation unless I ask \"explain this\"\n```\n\n---\n\nThis covers everything.                 "text": "\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nAlright, great \u2014 I have everything now. Here's the full honest picture:\n\n---\n\n## 1. What Google AI Studio Build Mode ACTUALLY Supports\n\nFor web apps, AI Studio creates a full-stack environment that includes a client-side web frontend (React is the default) and a server-side Node.js runtime that allows for secure API calls, database connections, and npm package usage.\n\nIn addition to React and Angular, Next.js apps are now supported out of the box \u2014 you select your framework in the Settings panel.\n\nSo the **supported frameworks are: React, Angular, Next.js.** That's it officially.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Can It Build Angular Frontend + NestJS Backend Separately? \u2014 Honest Answer\n\n**No. Not natively. Here's exactly why:**\n\nThe Antigravity Agent intelligently manages multiple files across your stack, ensuring that changes are propagated correctly \u2014 but the architecture is one unified full-stack environment per project, not two separate projects.\n\nThe backend runtime AI Studio spins up is **plain Node.js + Express**, not NestJS. By default AI Studio builds in React (Vite/Tailwind), but you can toggle the settings to use Angular. The backend layer does not have a framework toggle \u2014 it's always Node.js.\n\n**NestJS is NOT a selectable backend in AI Studio Build mode.** It's a Node.js framework that you'd have to ask the AI to write manually \u2014 and then it lives inside the same project container, not as a truly separate deployable service.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The Prototyping vs Production Reality\n\nThis is the most important thing for your project:\n\nAI Studio is for prototyping only. For production workloads, migrate to Vertex AI or implement proper backend architecture.\n\nMost founders start in AI Studio, then migrate to Vertex AI or custom infrastructure for production.\n\nFor a **KYC platform with RBAC+ABAC+ReBAC, live video streams, encrypted recordings, MongoDB Atlas, and 500+ roles** \u2014 AI Studio Build mode is **not your production tool.** It's a scaffolding tool.\n\n---\n\n## 4. The Right Workflow for Your Project\n\nHere's the honest recommended approach for what you're building:\n\n```\nPHASE 1 \u2014 Use AI Studio (Playground/Chat, NOT Build mode)\n\u2193  Use Gemini 2.5 Pro in Chat/Playground\n\u2193  Generate code module by module (Angular components, NestJS modules)\n\u2193  Copy code into your local IDE\n\nPHASE 2 \u2014 Build locally with your real stack\n\u2193  Angular 18 (frontend) \u2014 separate project\n\u2193  NestJS (backend) \u2014 separate project  \n\u2193  MongoDB Atlas (your existing DB)\n\u2193  Export/push to GitHub from AI Studio for handoff\n\nPHASE 3 \u2014 Deploy separately\n\u2193  Angular \u2192 Vercel / Nginx / Cloud Run\n\u2193  NestJS \u2192 Cloud Run / VPS / Docker\n```\n\n---\n\n## 5. So What Is the Custom Instructions Tab Actually For?\n\nSince you asked this specifically \u2014 and my last answer was wrong to give you a NestJS system prompt for it \u2014 here is what the **Custom Instructions in AI Studio Build mode actually does:**\n\nIt tells the **Antigravity Agent** how to behave when generating your app **within that single Build mode project.** It is NOT a cross-project memory. It applies only to one app session.\n\n**What to actually write there (correctly, for your Angular project in Build mode):**\n\n```\nYou are building a private enterprise KYC admin platform.\n\nFramework: Angular 18 with standalone components and Angular Material.\nBackend: Node.js with Express (server-side runtime).\nDatabase: Connect to MongoDB Atlas using the Mongoose npm package.\nAuth: JWT tokens in httpOnly cookies only. Never localStorage.\nSecurity: Always add input validation, rate limiting, and auth middleware.\nStyle: Angular Material dark theme. Admin dashboard layout with sidebar.\nCode quality: Always generate complete working code, no placeholders.\nNever ask for clarification \u2014 make the best decision and proceed.\nAlways handle errors. Never leave unhandled promises.\nWhen adding a feature, update both frontend and backend together.\n```\n\n---\n\n## 6. Your Angular + NestJS Question \u2014 The Real Answer\n\n**Yes, Angular + NestJS is the right combination for your project.** It's an industry-standard enterprise pairing. But for that combination:\n\n- Use **AI Studio Chat/Playground** (not Build mode) to generate the code\n- Or use **Cursor / VS Code with Gemini** via the exported GitHub project\n- Run **two separate projects** locally \u2014 Angular on port 4200, NestJS on port 3000\n- Connect them via REST API or WebSockets\n\nBuild mode is great for quick prototypes and demos \u2014 but your KYC system with the complexity you described needs a real local dev environment. AI Studio is the **code generator**, not the **development environment** for production-grade security apps.",

                                "is_missing": false,
                                "text": "I built a NestJS + Next.js monorepo I&#x27;d happily start any new SaaS on today. It&#x27;s on GitHub. The README covers what&#x27;s in it. This post is about three decisions that shaped how it&#x27;s organized, and why I think they&#x27;ll hold up as AI assistants keep getting better at writing code. The project uses Drizzle instead of Prisma, Base UI instead of Radix, and oxlint instead of ESLint. These aren&#x27;t adventurous picks. They share one property: they reduce the number of things that can go wrong. Drizzle&#x27;s schema is its type definition. You write pgTable(...), call $inferSelect, and you have a typed row object. No code generation step, no separate schema format, no runtime engine. When a column changes, I rebuild the database package and every consumer sees the new type. Prisma is excellent, but it asks you to maintain a parallel schema language. I&#x27;d rather have one.\n\nI built a NestJS + Next.js monorepo I'd happily start any new SaaS on today. It's on GitHub. \n\nThe... Tagged with turborepo, nestjs, nextjs.\n\nThe \"start simple, grow when the problem demands it\" philosophy is exactly right. We run NestJS across our entire payment platform and the biggest mistake we made early on was treating every service like it needed full DDD from day one. Some services just move money from A to B \u2014 they're glorified CRUD with compliance checks. Others handle retry logic, idempotency, and settlement state machines where every edge case matters. Your .claude/rules/ setup is interesting. We've gone a similar route \u2014 structured context files that the AI loads based on which service it's touching. The payoff isn't just productivity, it's consistency. Without those guardrails, AI agents drift toward their own defaults and the codebase slowly stops feeling like one team wrote it. One thing I'd add about Drizzle vs Prisma for payments specifically: Drizzle's \"schema is the type\" approach is brilliant when you have shared schemas across services.\n\n\n\nAuth & RBAC",

                        "text": "Alright, great \u2014 I have everything now. Here's the full honest picture:\n\n---\n\n## 1. What Google AI Studio Build Mode ACTUALLY Supports\n\nFor web apps, AI Studio creates a full-stack environment that includes a client-side web frontend (React is the default) and a server-side Node.js runtime that allows for secure API calls, database connections, and npm package usage.\n\nIn addition to React and Angular, Next.js apps are now supported out of the box \u2014 you select your framework in the Settings panel.\n\nSo the **supported frameworks are: React, Angular, Next.js.** That's it officially.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Can It Build Angular Frontend + NestJS Backend Separately? \u2014 Honest Answer\n\n**No. Not natively. Here's exactly why:**\n\nThe Antigravity Agent intelligently manages multiple files across your stack, ensuring that changes are propagated correctly \u2014 but the architecture is one unified full-stack environment per project, not two separate projects.\n\nThe backend runtime AI Studio spins up is **plain Node.js + Express**, not NestJS. By default AI Studio builds in React (Vite/Tailwind), but you can toggle the settings to use Angular. The backend layer does not have a framework toggle \u2014 it's always Node.js.\n\n**NestJS is NOT a selectable backend in AI Studio Build mode.** It's a Node.js framework that you'd have to ask the AI to write manually \u2014 and then it lives inside the same project container, not as a truly separate deployable service.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The Prototyping vs Production Reality\n\nThis is the most important thing for your project:\n\nAI Studio is for prototyping only. For production workloads, migrate to Vertex AI or implement proper backend architecture.\n\nMost founders start in AI Studio, then migrate to Vertex AI or custom infrastructure for production.\n\nFor a **KYC platform with RBAC+ABAC+ReBAC, live video streams, encrypted recordings, MongoDB Atlas, and 500+ roles** \u2014 AI Studio Build mode is **not your production tool.** It's a scaffolding tool.\n\n---\n\n## 4. The Right Workflow for Your Project\n\nHere's the honest recommended approach for what you're building:\n\n```\nPHASE 1 \u2014 Use AI Studio (Playground/Chat, NOT Build mode)\n\u2193  Use Gemini 2.5 Pro in Chat/Playground\n\u2193  Generate code module by module (Angular components, NestJS modules)\n\u2193  Copy code into your local IDE\n\nPHASE 2 \u2014 Build locally with your real stack\n\u2193  Angular 18 (frontend) \u2014 separate project\n\u2193  NestJS (backend) \u2014 separate project  \n\u2193  MongoDB Atlas (your existing DB)\n\u2193  Export/push to GitHub from AI Studio for handoff\n\nPHASE 3 \u2014 Deploy separately\n\u2193  Angular \u2192 Vercel / Nginx / Cloud Run\n\u2193  NestJS \u2192 Cloud Run / VPS / Docker\n```\n\n---\n\n## 5. So What Is the Custom Instructions Tab Actually For?\n\nSince you asked this specifically \u2014 and my last answer was wrong to give you a NestJS system prompt for it \u2014 here is what the **Custom Instructions in AI Studio Build mode actually does:**\n\nIt tells the **Antigravity Agent** how to behave when generating your app **within that single Build mode project.** It is NOT a cross-project memory. It applies only to one app session.\n\n**What to actually write there (correctly, for your Angular project in Build mode):**\n\n```\nYou are building a private enterprise KYC admin platform.\n\nFramework: Angular 18 with standalone components and Angular Material.\nBackend: Node.js with Express (server-side runtime).\nDatabase: Connect to MongoDB Atlas using the Mongoose npm package.\nAuth: JWT tokens in httpOnly cookies only. Never localStorage.\nSecurity: Always add input validation, rate limiting, and auth middleware.\nStyle: Angular Material dark theme. Admin dashboard layout with sidebar.\nCode quality: Always generate complete working code, no placeholders.\nNever ask for clarification \u2014 make the best decision and proceed.\nAlways handle errors. Never leave unhandled promises.\nWhen adding a feature, update both frontend and backend together.\n```\n\n---\n\n## 6. Your Angular + NestJS Question \u2014 The Real Answer\n\n**Yes, Angular + NestJS is the right combination for your project.** It's an industry-standard enterprise pairing. JWT stored in httpOnly cookie.\n- Database: None for this prototype\n- Recording: None for this prototype \u2014 live streaming only\n\nARCHITECTURE:\n- /app/page.tsx \u2014 landing/login page (choose role: admin or user)\n- /app/user/page.tsx \u2014 user KYC session page\n- /app/admin/page.tsx \u2014 admin dashboard page\n- /app/api/socket/route.ts \u2014 Socket.io signaling server\n- /app/api/auth/route.ts \u2014 hardcoded JWT auth endpoint\n- Socket.io server must run as a persistent Next.js custom server (server.ts)\n\nKYC USER FLOW:\n1. User lands on their page, clicks \"Start KYC\"\n2. Browser requests camera + microphone permission (getUserMedia)\n3. Browser requests GPS location permission (Geolocation API)\n4. WebRTC peer connection is created and offer is sent via Socket.io to admin\n5. User's live video + audio streams to admin in real time\n6. User's GPS coordinates sent via socket and displayed to admin on Leaflet map\n7. User sees a \"Waiting for admin...\" status and cannot proceed until admin acts\n\nADMIN FLOW:\n1. Admin logs in and sees a dashboard\n2. When a user starts KYC, admin sees an incoming session notification\n3. Admin sees: live video feed, live audio, GPS location on Leaflet map, session start time\n4. Admin has two buttons: \"Approve \u2705\" and \"Reject \u274c\"\n5. On approve/reject, a socket event is emitted to the user with the result\n6. User sees the result on their screen instantly\n\nSECURITY RULES:\n- JWT must be validated on every API route and socket connection\n- Admin route /app/admin must redirect to login if not admin role\n- User route /app/user must redirect to login if not user role\n- Never expose role logic on the client side \u2014 validate server side only\n- Camera/mic/location must always request explicit browser permission \u2014 never auto-access\n\nCODE RULES:\n- Always generate complete, working code \u2014 no TODOs, no placeholders\n- Use TypeScript throughout\n- Always handle permission denied errors for camera, mic, and location gracefully\n- Show clear UI feedback for every state: connecting, waiting, streaming, approved, rejected\n- Use Tailwind for all styling \u2014 clean dark admin UI\n- Never use localStorage for auth tokens \u2014 httpOnly cookies only\n- When generating a feature, always output all affected files together\n- Do not ask clarifying questions \u2014 make the best decision and build it\n```\n\n---\n\n## \ud83d\ude80 Your First Prompt to Type in Build Mode\n\nOnce custom instructions are saved, paste this as your **very first message:**\n\n```\nBuild a WebRTC KYC verification prototype in Next.js 14 with App Router and Tailwind CSS.\n\nStart with the complete project foundation:\n1.                 "uuid": "019fb87c-83de-7a70-90c5-a833b0cbc40a",
                "text": "Yes, this makes complete sense and it's actually the **right** UX decision. Here's why:\n\n**Homepage = Brand/Trust moment.** When a user lands, they should feel like they're dealing with something legitimate and serious \u2014 not immediately bombarded with permission popups. A clean, minimal homepage builds that trust first.\n\n**Consent screen = Separate, intentional step.** By navigating to a dedicated consent page, the user is making a conscious decision to proceed. This also has a legal advantage \u2014 it creates a clear, isolated consent moment which is important for KYC specifically. If consent and the action are on the same page, it feels rushed and looks unprofessional.\n\nSo your flow makes sense:\n\n```\nHomepage (clean, minimal, one CTA button)\n    \u2193\nConsent Screen (clearly lists what will be accessed \u2014 camera, mic, location \u2014 user agrees)\n    \u2193\nKYC Session (WebRTC starts only AFTER consent)\n```\n\nThis is actually how banks and financial institutions structure their KYC flows too \u2014 consent is always a separate, deliberate screen.\n\nWhat's your next doubt?",

                "uuid": "019fb87d-cff3-70fd-b615-00364c95ba89",
                "text": "Yes, makes sense for a prototype \u2014 skip the consent page, just get straight to testing the functionality.\n\nBut one practical heads-up: **browsers don't ask for all three permissions at once.** Chrome requests them one at a time, and also \u2014 **location permission is separate from camera/mic.** So the flow will naturally be:\n\n```\nUser opens homepage\n    \u2193\nChrome asks \u2192 Allow Camera & Microphone?  [Allow]\n    \u2193\nChrome asks \u2192 Allow Location?  [Allow]\n    \u2193\nSession starts automatically \u2192 streams to admin\n```\n\nAlso one important thing \u2014 **WebRTC with camera/mic only works on HTTPS or localhost.** Since you're testing on your smartphone, your phone and PC need to be either:\n\n- On the **same WiFi network** (local IP works), or\n- Deployed on **HTTPS** (even a free Vercel deployment works)\n\nOtherwise Chrome on mobile will block the camera/mic access entirely \u2014 not an AI Studio limitation, it's a browser security rule.\n\nSo just to confirm the prototype flow before you move on:\n\n- User opens the page \u2192 permissions auto-requested \u2192 stream starts \u2192 admin sees it live\n- Admin is on a **separate URL/page** that you open on your PC/another device\n- No login for prototype, just two direct URLs \u2014 one for user, one for admin?\n\nOr do you still want even a basic hardcoded login?",
                "content": [

                "text": "Yes, JWT works perfectly for this. And good thinking on hosting early \u2014 **Vercel** is the obvious choice here since you're on Next.js. Free tier, instant deployment, automatic HTTPS, and your phone will work with it out of the box. No configuration needed.\n\nSo the final prototype flow is clean:\n\n```\nUser Side (no auth)\nHomepage opens \u2192 Chrome requests camera + mic + location \u2192 stream starts \u2192 waiting for admin\n\nAdmin Side (JWT auth)\n/admin/login \u2192 hardcoded credentials \u2192 JWT issued \u2192 /admin/dashboard \u2192 sees live feed + location + approve/reject\n```\n\nOne thing worth clarifying though \u2014 JWT for admin works fine, but since this is Next.js you have two options for where the token lives:\n\n- **httpOnly cookie** \u2014 more secure, token never touches JavaScript, better practice\n- **localStorage** \u2014 simpler to implement but less secure\n\nFor a prototype that you're also considering hosting, I'd say go with **httpOnly cookie** from the start. It's not much extra work and you won't have to redo it later when you go production.\n\nDoes that work for you? And one more thing \u2014 for the admin dashboard, do you want the live user sessions to appear automatically when a user connects, or should the admin manually refresh/check?",

                "uuid": "019fb8a0-fd45-76b8-aa12-84e3cffcafce",
                "text": "Yes, this is absolutely possible and it's a brilliant solution actually. Very practical for a solo admin setup. Let me confirm the full flow:\n\n**Admin Offline Flow:**\n```\nUser connects \u2192 socket detects admin is offline\n\u2192 Socket sends browser notification to admin \n  (Chrome push notification \u2014 even if tab is in background)\n\u2192 User sees a minimal \"Please wait, connecting you to admin...\"\n  with a subtle 120 second countdown (not too obvious, just a small indicator)\n```\n\n**Two outcomes after 120 seconds:**\n\n```\nOutcome 1 \u2014 Admin comes online within 120s:\n\u2192 Countdown disappears silently\n\u2192 Session starts normally as if nothing happened\n\u2192 User never knew there was an issue\n\nOutcome 2 \u2014 Admin doesn't come online in 120s:\n\u2192 User sees:\n  \"Admin is currently unavailable\"\n  \"Would you like to record a message instead?\"\n\u2192 User clicks record\n\u2192 Camera/mic already active (permissions already granted)\n\u2192 User records video of themselves + documents (no time limit)\n\u2192 Submits \u2192 stored in MongoDB\n\u2192 User sees \"Your message has been sent, \n   admin will review it shortly\"\n\u2192 Admin gets notification of recorded message when they come online\n```\n\n**Tech behind it:**\n```\nChrome Push Notifications \u2192 Web Push API + service worker\n120s countdown \u2192 simple server side socket timer\nVideo recording \u2192 MediaRecorder API \n  (camera/mic already active so no extra permissions needed)\nRecorded video storage \u2192 MongoDB GridFS \n  (handles large video files in chunks)\n```\n\nThis is completely possible and honestly very well thought out. The fact that camera/mic permissions are already granted by the time the 120s kicks in makes the recording flow seamless \u2014 no extra steps for the user at all.\n\nDoes this match what you had in mind?",

                "text": "Perfect, all noted. Now let me explain the STUN server in simple terms:\n\n---\n\n### What is a STUN Server?\n\nThink of it this way \u2014\n\nYour phone and your PC are both connected to the same WiFi, but they don't know each other's **exact network address** to send video directly to each other. They know their **local IP** (like 192.168.1.5) but WebRTC needs to figure out the **best path** to send data between two devices.\n\nA STUN server is basically a **middleman that just answers one question:**\n\n> \"Hey, what does my connection look like from the outside world?\"\n\n```\nYour Phone \u2192 asks STUN server \u2192 \"what's my public address?\"\nSTUN server \u2192 replies \u2192 \"you look like X.X.X.X to the outside\"\nPhone shares that info with PC via Socket.io\nPC does the same\nNow they know how to reach each other directly\nSTUN server's job is done \u2014 it leaves the conversation\n```\n\n**Important:** STUN server does NOT carry your video. It only helps devices **find each other**. After that the video flows directly phone \u2194 PC (peer to peer).\n\n**For your prototype** \u2014 Google provides a free STUN server:\n```\nstun:stun.l.google.com:19302\n```\nThis one line in the WebRTC config is all you need. No setup, no cost, just works.\n\n---\n\n### When would STUN fail?\n\nOnly if you're on a very strict corporate/university network that blocks peer connections. Your home WiFi \u2014 it'll work perfectly.\n\n---\n\nNow all points are addressed. Summary of decisions made:\n\n```\nUser identity \u2192 skip for prototype\nMultiple users \u2192 admin identifies by feed visually\nSTUN server \u2192 Google's free STUN server\nUser disconnects \u2192 show \"User disconnected\" on admin grid\nAdmin disconnects \u2192 show \"Admin disconnected\" on user screen\nRecorded video \u2192 120 seconds max\n               \u2192 compressed for storage (minimal size)\n               \u2192 decompressed to original quality on playback\nChat file size \u2192 no limit for admin\nSnapshot \u2192 stored in MongoDB as compressed image\n         \u2192 used only for cross-verification disputes\n```\n\nAre we good to move forward or anything else to discuss?",
